195 FERC ¶ 61,210
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Before Commissioners:  Laura V. Swett, Chairman;
                                        David Rosner, Lindsay S. See,
                                        Judy W. Chang, and David LaCerte.


ORDER ACCEPTING TARIFF REVISIONS, SUBJECT TO CONDITION

(Issued June 18, 2026)

On April 4, 2025, as amended on September 26, 2025, Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO) submitted, pursuant to section 205 of the Federal Power Act (FPA) and part 35 of the Commission’s regulations, proposed revisions to its Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff (Tariff) to implement reforms, beginning with the 2028/2029 Planning Year, to improve the real-time visibility and the efficient procurement and operation of demand-side resources and certain supply-side resources that elect to participate during Emergencies.  In this order, we accept MISO’s proposed Tariff revisions, subject to condition, effective September 1, 2027, as requested, and direct MISO to submit a compliance filing within 30 days of the date of this order.
Background
Demand-side Resources in MISO
MISO identifies two major types of demand-side resources within its markets:  Demand Resources and behind the meter generation resources.  Demand Resources can be a singular asset (e.g., industrial facility), aggregations of resources (e.g., households), or other programs that are used to enhance grid reliability, reduce peak Demand, and provide capacity in MISO’s markets.  Behind the meter generation resources encompass any type of generation resource located behind a Commercial Pricing Node (CPNode).
Demand-side resources may currently participate in MISO’s markets through four options.  The first option, Demand Response Resource (DRR), permits demand-side resources that interrupt or control Demand to participate as supply-side resources in MISO’s energy markets, pursuant to Order Nos. 719 and 745, and receive compensation in the form of Locational Marginal Price (LMP).  DRR is split into two categories, DRR-Type I and DRR-Type II, both of which may also participate in MISO’s capacity market.  The second option, Load Modifying Resource (LMR), includes demand-side resources that only participate in MISO’s capacity market and are obligated to respond to an Emergency when called upon by MISO.  The third option, Emergency Demand Response (EDR), includes demand-side resources that voluntarily offer to respond to MISO instructions during an Emergency.  Under the fourth option, demand-side resources may dual register as DRR-Type I to provide energy and LMR to provide capacity.
Prior MISO Demand-side Resource Reforms
MISO has previously proposed a series of Tariff filings to implement incremental reforms to LMRs as part of MISO’s Resource Availability and Need (RAN) initiative.  On February 19, 2019, the Commission accepted MISO’s proposal to require that, beginning with the 2019/2020 Planning Year, LMRs must offer capability based on actual availability in all Seasons, not only in the Summer, and also be available based on the shortest notification requirement that an LMR could consistently meet within a 12-hour window.  On March 29, 2019, the Commission accepted MISO’s proposal to require LMRs to conduct an annual real power test beginning with the 2020/2021 Planning Year.  On August 14, 2020, the Commission accepted MISO’s proposal, beginning with the 2022/2023 Planning Year to, among other things, accredit LMRs for capacity in the Planning Resource Auction (Auction) and to decrease the maximum notification time for LMRs from 12 hours to six hours.
The Commission has also considered MISO proposals that relate more broadly to demand-side resources.  On July 18, 2025, the Commission accepted MISO’s proposal to revise the participation requirements associated with demand-side resources, beginning with the 2026/2027 Planning Year, to prevent or reduce:  (1) payment for nonexistent or overstated curtailments; (2) inaccurate or inflated baselines on which curtailments are based; and (3) fraudulent registration of resources.  MISO proposed these revisions in response to four Commission orders finding that certain owners of demand-side resources in MISO engaged in market manipulation and fraud.  On the same day, the Commission accepted MISO’s proposal to remove the ability for demand-side resources to dual register as both EDR and either DRR or LMR, also beginning with the 2026/2027 Planning Year.  Additionally, on November 17, 2025, the Commission accepted MISO’s proposal to require all Demand Resources to submit evidence of a real power test beginning with the 2026/2027 Planning Year.
Prior MISO Resource Accreditation Reforms
MISO has also proposed broader RAN-related filings affecting demand-side resources.  On August 31, 2022, the Commission accepted MISO’s Seasonal Accredited Capacity (SAC) proposal to shift from an annual resource adequacy construct based on the Summer peak to a four-Season construct beginning with the 2023/2024 Planning Year.  The accreditation changes established in the SAC Order, as provided for in Schedule 53, measure the historical resource-level performance of dispatchable thermal resources and certain DRRs using a deterministic element.  Subsequently, on October 25, 2024, the Commission accepted MISO’s proposal to enhance the Schedule 53 methodology by adding a probabilistic element, thus creating the two-step Direct Loss of Load (DLOL) methodology under new Schedule 53A, which MISO will use to determine SAC values for all Capacity Resources participating in the Auction beginning with the 2028/2029 Planning Year.
Under the DLOL methodology, MISO will first calculate the combined expected availability and performance of all Schedule 53A Resources within a Resource Class during certain hours that reflect periods of highest system risk from MISO’s Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) study to determine Resource Class-level Unforced Capacity (UCAP).  This probabilistic element aligns Resource Class-level accreditation with
 
the Planning Reserve Margin Requirements (Reserve Requirements) that each Load Serving Entity (LSE) must meet to be considered resource adequate for each Season during the applicable Planning Year.  Second, MISO will allocate the Resource Class-level UCAP among individual resources in a specific Resource Class using historical individual resource performance during Resource Adequacy (RA) Hours, which represent the periods of highest risk and greatest need.  The RA Hours for each Season include a 65-hour target, representing the tightest 3% of hours in a Season consisting of all hours with Maximum Generation Events (MaxGen Events) and any remaining hours with the tightest operating margin, subject to a maximum operating margin threshold of 25%.  If there are fewer than 65 hours identified for a Season after including eligible hours up to the 25% operating margin threshold, a Seasonal RA Hours Deficiency exists.
MISO accredits resources based on the Intermediate Seasonal Accredited Capacity (ISAC), which is determined using the real-time offered availability, capped at the resource’s Generation Verification Test Capacity value, during Seasonal non-RA Hours (Tier 1) and Seasonal RA Hours (Tier 2).  The ISAC value is a weighted average of Tier 1 hours at 20% and Tier 2 hours at 80%.  The ISAC value is then converted to a resource’s final SAC value by applying a system-wide UCAP/ISAC ratio.
Filing
MISO proposes Tariff revisions to improve the real-time visibility and the efficient procurement and operation of DRRs, LMRs, and behind the meter generation resources, including updating the accreditation of such resources, pursuant to newly proposed Schedule 53B, to align with the DLOL methodology used to accredit supply-side resources under Schedule 53A.  MISO explains that the demand-side resources subject to the instant proposal account for approximately 12 GW of capacity, the majority of which MISO relies on before involuntary load shed.  MISO asserts, however, that the disparate patchwork of legacy demand-side resource programs that MISO has stitched together over the past two decades is no longer sufficient to address ongoing transformations in the electric utility industry, which makes the MISO region increasingly vulnerable to multiple reliability risks.
MISO further proposes to update the accreditation of Available Max Emergency Resources (AME Resource), which are supply-side resources that have elected to participate during Emergencies, pursuant to Schedule 53B.  MISO explains that AME Resources are included as part of the instant proposal to ensure the alignment and equitable treatment of resources participating in MISO’s capacity market.
According to MISO, the instant proposal has three objectives:  (1) improve operational effectiveness by accessing LMRs with longer notification times earlier in the Emergency process, thus reserving LMRs with shorter notification times for later steps in MISO’s Emergency Operating Procedures, and also integrating LMRs into the unit commitment process; (2) accredit demand-side resources based on their availability to ensure that demand-side resource accreditation reflects how often those resources respond to Emergencies and the level at which they perform; and (3) refine meter data requirements and MISO-initiated test requirements to better verify and measure performance.  MISO organizes its proposal into five elements:  (1) participation options; (2) measurement and verification; (3) real-time availability; (4) accreditation; and (5) testing.
MISO states that the instant proposal balances MISO’s operational needs with the diverse demand-side programs and unique characteristics of the underlying resources participating in MISO’s markets.  MISO asserts that, in seeking this balance, the instant proposal evolved through extensive stakeholder feedback that resulted in a final accreditation design that is necessarily complex but reasonably accommodates the competing needs of both MISO and its stakeholders.  Accordingly, MISO explains that the final design creates non-discriminatory participation options for all demand-side resources that wish to participate in MISO’s markets, and that these demand-side resources are accredited in a way that reflects their operational characteristics and unique capabilities.  As part of the instant proposal, MISO includes an affidavit from Potomac Economics, Ltd., MISO’s independent market monitor (IMM), that generally supports MISO’s proposal.
MISO requests an effective date of September 1, 2027, to align the accreditation of demand-side resources with the DLOL-based accreditation of Schedule 53A Resources, beginning with the 2028/2029 Planning Year.  MISO states that it recognizes that its requested effective date is beyond 120 days from the date of its filing, and, therefore requests waiver of section 35.3(a) of the Commission’s regulations, asserting that its effective date is intended to provide regulatory certainty to both stakeholders and MISO with respect to the Tariff provisions applicable to the 2028/2029 Planning Year well in advance of the Auction that will be held in the Spring of 2028.  
Notice of Filing and Responsive Pleadings
Notice of the filing was published in the Federal Register, 90 Fed. Reg. 15462 (Apr. 11, 2025), with interventions and protests due on or before May 5, 2025.
Notices of intervention were filed by:  the Louisiana Public Service Commission; the Michigan Public Service Commission; and Organization of MISO States, Inc. (OMS).
Timely motions to intervene were filed by:  Advanced Energy United (Advanced Energy); ALLETE, Inc. (ALLETE); Alliant Energy Corporate Services, Inc.; Ameren Services Company (Ameren); American Electric Power Service Corporation (AEP); American Municipal Power, Inc. (AMP); Arkansas Electric Cooperative Corporation; Association of Businesses Advocating Tariff Equity; Calpine Corporation; Central Minnesota Municipal Power Agency (CMMPA); Cleco Power LLC; Coalition of Midwest Power Producers (COMPP); Coalition of MISO Transmission Customers; Consumers Energy Company; Cooperative Energy; DTE Electric Company (DTE Electric); Enerwise Global Technologies, LLC; Entergy Services, LLC (Entergy Services) on behalf of the Entergy Operating Companies; Great Lakes Utilities, Madison Gas and Electric Company, Missouri Joint Municipal Electric Utility Commission, Missouri River Energy Services, and WPPI Energy (together, Midwest TDUs); Hoosier Energy Rural Electric Cooperative, Inc.; Illinois Industrial Energy Consumers; Illinois Municipal Electric Agency (IMEA); Lansing Board of Water and Light (Lansing Board); Louisiana Energy Users Group; Michigan Public Power Agency (MPPA); MidAmerican Energy Company; Midwest Large Energy Consumers; Northwestern Wisconsin Electric Company (NWECO); Otter Tail Power Company; Steel Producers; Upper Midwest Municipal Energy Group (UMMEG); Vistra Corp. and Dynegy Marketing and Trade, LLC; Voltus, Inc. (Voltus); Wisconsin Electric Power Company, Wisconsin Public Service Corporation, and Upper Michigan Energy Resources Corporation (together, WEC Utilities); and Xcel Energy Services Inc. (Xcel Energy).
Comments and protests were filed by:  Advanced Energy; ALLETE; AMP; BTMG Utilities; COMPP; DTE Electric; Entergy Services; IMEA; Midwest TDUs; OMS; Steel Producers; and Voltus.
On June 26, 2025, MISO filed an answer (MISO Answer).  On July 11, 2025, Midwest TDUs filed an answer to the MISO Answer (Midwest TDUs Answer).  On July 14, 2025, BTMG Utilities filed an answer to the MISO Answer (BTMG Utilities Answer).
A deficiency letter was issued on September 8, 2025, to request additional information (Deficiency Letter).  On September 26, 2025, MISO filed a response to the Deficiency Letter (Deficiency Response).  Notice of the Deficiency Response was published in the Federal Register, 90 Fed. Reg. 47303 (Oct. 1, 2025), with interventions and protests due on or before October 17, 2025.  Midwest TDUs filed a protest (Midwest TDUs Deficiency Response Protest).
Discussion
Procedural Matters
Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.214 (2025), the notices of intervention and timely, unopposed motions to intervene serve to make the entities that filed them parties to this proceeding.
Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (2025), prohibits an answer to a protest or answer unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.  We accept the answers filed by MISO, Midwest TDUs, and BTMG Utilities because they have provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process.
Substantive Matters
As explained in further detail below, we accept MISO’s proposed Tariff revisions, effective September 1, 2027, as requested, subject to condition, and direct MISO to submit a compliance filing within 30 days of the date of this order.
Participation Options
MISO’s Filing
MISO states that demand-side resources can currently participate in MISO’s markets as DRR-Type I, DRR-Type II, LMR, and EDR.  MISO proposes to split LMRs into two distinct types, LMR-Type I and LMR-Type II, and add a new Non-Emergency BTMG participation option such that demand-side resources participating under the proposed design will have the following participation options:  (1) DRR-Type I; (2) DRR-Type II; (3) LMR-Type I; (4) LMR-Type II; (5) Non-Emergency BTMG; and (6) EDR.  MISO explains that the different options allow for participation in MISO’s markets depending on market participants’ goals, the type and operating characteristics of market participants’ resources, and market participants’ ability to fulfill the requirements of a participation option.  MISO states that each participation option has specific obligations and compensation mechanisms that do not depend on the type of resource, which creates non-discriminatory participation options for all resources and accredits them in a way that reflects their operational characteristics and unique capabilities.  MISO further states that each participation option in which market participants currently engage will continue to be permissible under MISO’s proposal, but that MISO is revising these existing options to include detailed qualification requirements, obligations, and deployment information.
MISO explains that, as all participation options are eligible to receive capacity payments, a market participant considering which option to select should decide whether to also participate in MISO’s energy markets, thus receiving energy payments in the form of LMP.  MISO states that a demand-side resource participating in MISO’s energy markets and receiving energy payments is classified as an economic resource, whereas a resource participating only in MISO’s capacity market and receiving capacity payments is classified as a reliability resource.  MISO explains, therefore, that a Demand Resource can participate economically as DRR-Type I or DRR-Type II, or, alternatively, as a reliability resource through the LMR-Type I and LMR-Type II options.  Additionally, MISO states that behind the meter generation resources may participate economically as DRR-Type I or DRR-Type II, or as reliability resources through the LMR-Type I, LMR-Type II, or Non-Emergency BTMG options.
MISO further explains that market participants should determine whether they wish to have an obligation for their resources to perform only during Emergencies or to be capable of performing at any time.  MISO notes that non-Emergency resources are expected to perform like supply-side resources while Emergency resources are deployed to reduce Demand during, or in anticipation of, periods when system conditions are tight and reliability concerns arise.  MISO states that, under its proposal, Demand Resources that participate as DRR-Type I or LMR are Emergency resources while Demand Resources that participate as DRR-Type II are non-Emergency resources.  MISO explains that, for behind the meter generation resources, the DRR-Type I and LMR options require Emergency-only participation while the Non-Emergency BTMG option allows resources to participate during Emergencies, but without an obligation to respond to MISO instructions.  Additionally, MISO states that it will require behind the meter generation resources to wait three Planning Years after registering before switching between Emergency and Non-Emergency participation.  According to MISO, this waiting period prevents such resources from switching back and forth to maximize accreditation without precluding them from switching into MISO’s energy markets at any time.
MISO states that the proposed suite of participation options ensures more timely and predictable Demand reduction when Emergencies arise.  MISO explains that, under its proposed deployment order, MISO would first call on DRR-Type I, which must respond within six hours, and deploy such resources based on economic merit order.  MISO states that it would next call on LMR-Type I, which also must respond within six hours, and deploy such resources based on locational requirements and lead time (i.e., long-lead resources before short-lead resources) at the beginning of a MaxGen Warning declaration.  MISO explains that, despite having identical performance requirements, DRR-Type I is deployed prior to LMR-Type I in exchange for receiving energy payments.  MISO states that, lastly, it would call on LMR-Type II, which must respond within 30 minutes, at the beginning of an EEA-Level 2 declaration.  MISO asserts, therefore, that its proposal ensures that resources relied upon during Emergencies can effectively support grid reliability when needed.
DRR-Type I and DRR-Type II
As discussed above, MISO states that DRR-Type I and DRR-Type II currently permit demand-side resources to participate as supply-side resources in MISO’s energy markets, thus receiving compensation in the form of LMP, and may also participate in MISO’s capacity market.  MISO notes, however, that DRR-Type I is a committable option, meaning that resources provide all or nothing energy, whereas DRR-Type II is a dispatchable option where resources must be able to provide incremental amounts of energy.  MISO further distinguishes DRR-Type II by noting that this option has Applicable Reliability Standards and an obligation to offer into the Day-Ahead Market.
MISO explains that, under its proposal, Demand Resources and behind the meter generation resources can participate economically as DRR-Type I or DRR-Type II.  Accordingly, MISO proposes minor revisions to the existing definitions of DRR-Type I and DRR-Type II to replace:  (1) “Behind the Meter Generation,” which is a Tariff-defined term, with “behind the meter generation;” and (2) “controllable Load” with “Demand Resource,” which clarifies that such eligible resources must be capable of taking actions to voluntarily, actively, and temporarily adjust Demand in response to MISO instructions.
MISO further proposes to revise the existing performance requirements of DRR-Type I to make them identical to those that MISO proposes for LMR-Type I.  In particular, MISO proposes to allow DRR-Type I to be:  (1) offered as Zonal Resource Credits in the Auction; (2) used in a Fixed Resource Adequacy Plan; or (3) used in a Reliability Based Demand Curve Opt-Out, all practices currently applicable to LMRs, which would require all DRR-Type I to be available for use in an Emergency unless replaced with other Zonal Resource Credits.  While MISO also proposes to remove DRR-Type I from the list of eligible Capacity Resources, MISO explains that DRR-Type I may still qualify to register in the Auction and participate in MISO’s capacity market if such resources:  (1) have a response time of six hours or less; (2) sustain load reduction for at least four continuous hours; and (3) are subject to testing, verification, and the penalty provisions currently applicable to LMRs in the case of non-performance.
MISO proposes to eliminate the current practice of allowing market participants to dual register as DRR and LMR because the proposed DRR-Type I option has the same performance requirements as the proposed LMR-Type I option.  Thus, MISO states that, under its proposal, market participants retain the obligations of a DRR-Type I dual-registered as an LMR without the need for dual registration.  Moreover, MISO states that eliminating dual registration will ease the administrative burden for both market participants and MISO when tracking the performance obligations of resources that currently dual register as DRR-Type I and LMR.
Additionally, MISO proposes Tariff revisions to clarify that DRR-Type II backed by a Demand Resource or a behind the meter generation resource are eligible to qualify as Capacity Resources provided that a market participant registers such resources with MISO for the upcoming Planning Year.  Moreover, MISO proposes new Tariff language to require that a DRR-Type II backed by a Demand Resource that wishes to qualify as a Capacity Resource shall:  (1) demonstrate an existing resource’s capability to MISO no later than October 31 prior to the Planning Year, unless MISO provides an extension; or (2) submit test data to MISO for new resources, or resources with an increase in capacity, prior to qualification, but no later than March 1 prior to the Auction.
LMR-Type I and LMR-Type II
MISO proposes to revise the existing definition of LMR to separately establish and define LMR-Type I and LMR-Type II.  MISO explains that, under its proposal, LMR-Type I and LMR-Type II are Emergency-only, reliability participation options whereby Demand Resources and BTMG that can sustain load reduction for at least four continuous hours can participate in the Auction.  MISO proposes to deploy LMR-Type I and LMR-Type II during Emergencies based on resources’ notification times such that longer-lead resources will be considered for deployment before shorter-lead resources.  Specifically, MISO explains that LMR-Type I will be deployed during, or in anticipation of, a MaxGen Warning declaration and must be capable of reducing Demand within six hours or less when called.  MISO states that, in contrast, LMR-Type II must be capable of reducing Demand within 30 minutes or less when deployed during, or in anticipation of, an EEA-Level 2 declaration.  Additionally, MISO proposes that, in the case of non-performance, LMR-Type I and LMR-Type II will be subject to the testing, verification, and penalty provisions currently applicable to LMRs.
MISO states that, while LMR-Type I may choose to be unavailable for deployment in exchange for reduced accreditation, LMR-Type II must be available for deployment during Emergencies.  MISO explains that the flexibility afforded to LMR-Type I is intentionally not afforded to LMR-Type II to incentivize resources to exchange payment and flexibility for deployment order.  Additionally, MISO explains that it initially considered limiting LMR participation to resources with a response time of 30 minutes or less, but that stakeholder preference for a participation option that permitted longer-lead time resources to only participate in the capacity market led MISO to develop the LMR-Type I option.  MISO further explains that it also placed the deployment of LMR-Type I at the MaxGen Warning stage of Emergency operations in response to stakeholder feedback.  MISO asserts that, because approximately half of EEA-Level 2 declarations have less than one hour between the declaration and the start of the event, requiring LMR-Type II to be deployable within 30 minutes ensures that these resources are always available when needed.
Non-Emergency BTMG
MISO proposes Tariff revisions to define Non-Emergency BTMG, which MISO states is a new participation option for behind the meter generation resources that serve Load intermittently or on a continual basis behind a CPNode.  MISO states that the introduction of the Non-Emergency BTMG option allows behind the meter generation resources without any Emergency obligations to participate as reliability resources, which will incentivize performance during Emergencies, thus reducing uncertainty in availability.  MISO further proposes new Tariff section 69A.3.10 to provide for the eligibility requirements for Non-Emergency BTMG, which include ownership limitations, prohibition on dual registration, restrictions on switching between Emergency and Non-Emergency designations, and specifications for testing and monitoring.  MISO asserts that this rule set is necessary because Non-Emergency BTMG have different operating and performance characteristics than BTMG.
Responsive Pleadings
Comments in Support
COMPP and DTE Electric argue that MISO’s proposed participation options will lead to more resources that are available and capable of responding to MISO instructions during periods of high system risk.  Additionally, COMPP and OMS contend that the range of participation options will provide operational flexibility to market participants.
COMPP, DTE Electric, and OMS also support MISO’s proposal to split LMRs into two distinct options.  COMPP and DTE Electric argue that bifurcating LMRs would allow resources with shorter lead times to respond only as a last resort, thus better aligning resource deployment with system needs.  Moreover, DTE Electric and OMS note that MISO proposed this reform following stakeholder feedback, which OMS asserts was a dramatic improvement over MISO’s initial design and was crucial to OMS’s general support of MISO’s proposal.
Additionally, COMPP asserts that eliminating the dual registration option for DRRs and LMRs will enhance MISO’s ability to monitor the performance and availability of resources, thus furthering MISO’s goal of improving the operation of Demand Resources, safeguarding the integrity of the market, and preventing manipulation.
Protests
Reduced Participation
Multiple protesters contend that MISO’s proposed participation options, if implemented, may limit, exclude, or otherwise disincentivize demand-side resources from participating in MISO’s markets.  IMEA and OMS note that LSEs rely on demand-side resources as part of MISO’s capacity resource mix, and MISO’s proposal may make demand response programs run by LSEs more burdensome, costly, and difficult to explain to participating resources.  ALLETE asserts that MISO’s proposal does not create the needed level of options and granularity to adequately compensate demand-side resources.  Entergy Services argues that, while it agrees with MISO that performance-based accreditation is appropriate to incentivize action, MISO should consider the wide range of resources under its umbrella such that, even if a resource’s participation may be limited, that resource is not excluded outright.  Steel Producers express concern with the complexity of MISO’s proposal, which they argue would change every way in which Demand Resources interact with MISO’s markets.  Steel Producers assert that MISO’s speed and piecemeal approach makes it difficult to holistically evaluate the justness and reasonableness of MISO’s proposal.
DRR-Type I and DRR-Type II
Midwest TDUs argue that MISO’s proposal eliminates all options for DRR-Type I with notification requirements longer than six hours to participate in MISO’s capacity and energy markets.  Midwest TDUs claim that, prior to MISO’s proposal, DRR-Type I was eligible to qualify as a Capacity Resource that could dual register as an LMR and participate in MISO’s energy markets.  Midwest TDUs assert, however, that the proposed Tariff revisions prevent dual registration and impose a new requirement that Demand Resources have a notification time less than or equal to six hours to register in the Auction as DRR-Type I.  Additionally, Midwest TDUs claim that current DRR-Type I, when backed by demand response, would no longer be able to participate as DRR-Type II because the proposed Tariff revisions require DRR-Type II to be “capable of complying with [MISO’s] Setpoint Instructions,” but resources that have previously used DRR-Type I have only two output states:  “on” or “off.”  Midwest TDUs argue that, because MISO does not acknowledge this significant change, let alone demonstrate that it is just and reasonable, MISO should explain what options have been preserved for DRR-Type I with lead times longer than six hours.  Midwest TDUs further argue that, if there are no options, the Commission should require MISO to revise its proposed Tariff language to allow such resources to continue participating in MISO’s markets.
Midwest TDUs also claim that MISO’s proposal contains conflicting testimony on whether, or to what extent, DRR-Type I has a must offer requirement.  Midwest TDUs assert that MISO proposes to remove DRR-Type I from the definition of Capacity Resources, which would also remove DRR-Type I from the category of resources with a must offer requirement.  Moreover, Midwest TDUs note that MISO states that DRR-Type I “do[es] not have the same must offer obligation” as Schedule 53A Resources and DRR-Type II, but that the IMM suggests that DRR-Type I has a must offer requirement.  Midwest TDUs therefore request that MISO confirm that DRR-Type I is not subject to a must offer requirement, consistent with the proposed Tariff language.
Voltus asserts that the requirement for a market participant registering a DRR to provide the Elemental Pricing Node (EPNode) information for each facility underlying the DRR is burdensome as this information must be obtained from the relevant Load Balancing Authority (LBA), which is not required by MISO to share this information with an Aggregator of Retail Customers (ARC).  Voltus argues that, until this facet of enrollment is addressed, it remains impossible for ARCs to be in full control of whether their enrollments will be accepted by MISO.  Accordingly, Voltus argues that MISO should resolve this issue in order for DRR-Type I and DRR-Type II to serve as suitable alternatives for market participants.
LMR-Type I and LMR-Type II
AMP argues that the proposed definitions of LMR-Type I and LMR-Type II are unnecessarily restrictive because they provide that qualifying resources must be owned by a single LSE or ARC.  AMP asserts that MISO, by failing to accommodate LMRs other than those owned by one entity, appears to preclude LMRs that may be leased or owned by a third-party and subject to an offtake agreement.  AMP further asserts that the proposed LMR definitions may preclude participation by LSEs that jointly own, or contractually control the output of, LMRs through ownership structures that are not captured in the Tariff definition of LSE.  AMP claims that MISO provides no support for limiting participation only to LMRs that are wholly-owned or serve a single LSE, and that this restriction does not comport with existing commercial or contractual practices.  AMP contends that MISO could address this issue by revising the definitions of LMR-Type I and LMR-Type II such that they apply to “[a] resource registered by a[n] [LSE] or an ARC,” but, as currently proposed, the limitations render MISO’s filing unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.
ALLETE and Midwest TDUs question whether MISO’s intent to call on LMR-Type I during the MaxGen Warning stage, which Midwest TDUs assert is three stages earlier than when MISO calls on LMRs under its current Emergency Operating Procedures, is just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory.  ALLETE and Midwest TDUs contend that calling on resources earlier and more frequently (as they allege the proposal will do) would have significant cost and operational implications, which, according to ALLETE, would result in unjust and unreasonable rates because Demand Resources would need to either cease providing services or increase their costs, either of which, in turn, would increase LSEs’ costs to secure capacity and result in higher customer rates.  While Midwest TDUs support MISO’s approach of calling first on LMR-Type I with longer lead-times, Midwest TDUs argue that the information in MISO’s proposal falls far short of demonstrating that deploying LMR-Type I at the MaxGen Warning stage is just and reasonable.  Moreover, Midwest TDUs assert that, because MISO’s proposal does not include Tariff revisions to call on LMR-Type I at the MaxGen Warning stage, the Commission should make clear that accepting MISO’s proposal does not constitute approval of MISO’s intent to call on LMR-Type I at this earlier stage.  Instead, Midwest TDUs argue that MISO should be directed to continue addressing this issue with stakeholders to ensure that the deployment order of LMRs is just and reasonable.
ALLETE and IMEA argue that changing the current two-hour notification for LMRs to the proposed 30-minute notification for LMR-Type II is a significant barrier to the continued participation of certain industrial resources.  ALLETE and IMEA assert that many resources have substantial safety and process continuity concerns that they must address prior to reducing load, and, further, that operational factors such as units’ size, age, and startup complexity restrict how quickly load can be curtailed.  IMEA further argues that requiring LMR-Type II to respond to Emergencies within 30 minutes is unreasonable because LMRs have historically been available, and have adequately performed, under the status quo.  IMEA claims that isolated instances of energy Emergencies where MISO is still able to maintain its system are not indicative of a need for LMRs to reduce load within 30 minutes, and, moreover, that from 2023 to present, MISO has not declared a system-wide Emergency declaration exceeding a Capacity Advisory Warning.  IMEA therefore asserts that MISO should increase the LMR-Type II response time to 90 minutes or more.  ALLETE similarly requests that the Commission require MISO to retain an option for resources to have a two-hour notice.
Additional Issues

Answers
MISO Answer
As an initial matter, MISO asserts that certain commenters largely or entirely support MISO’s proposal, and many either agree with the general direction of MISO’s proposal or, at a minimum, agree that reforms are needed to improve reliability. Thus, MISO requests that the Commission evaluate MISO’s proposal based on its merits, rather than accept that the complexity is inherently problematic, because the proposal accommodates the competing needs of both MISO and its stakeholders.

This will reclassify DRR-Type I to be a specific type of Planning Resource with a must offer requirement limited to emergencies,” but rather to the fact that a DRR-Type I must offer for at least one Emergency per Season, and that, for any additional Seasons in which a DRR-Type I does not offer, the resource would be subject to accreditation reductions.  MISO submits that this element of its proposal is just and reasonable and should be adopted without modification.
In response to Midwest TDUs’ claim that MISO proposes to eliminate all options for DRR-Type I with notification times longer than six hours to participate in both the capacity and energy markets, MISO argues that this description is inconsistent with the Tariff. MISO clarifies that there is no proposed change from the Tariff requirements currently imposed on resources, and that dual registration does not currently provide, nor is it intended to provide, any mechanism for a resource with a notification time exceeding six hours to register as an LMR.  Thus, MISO asserts that Midwest TDUs are mistaken and their concerns should be rejected.
In response to AMP’s concerns that the definitions of LMR-Type I and LMR-Type II should be revised to accommodate multiple ownership structures, MISO asserts that AMP relies on an unreasonably narrow definition of the term “own” that implies direct corporate ownership rather than a right of control or use.  MISO argues that, under any ordinary construction, the proposed definitions of LMR-Type I and LMR-Type II are sufficient to contemplate the hypothetical ownership structures identified by AMP.
In response to arguments from ALLETE and Midwest TDUs that it is not just and reasonable to move the deployment of LMR-Type I into the MaxGen Warning stage, MISO asserts that it addressed these concerns in the stakeholder process.  Specifically, MISO explains that stakeholder feedback and input from the IMM led to key design changes as MISO developed its proposal, including moving the deployment of LMR-Type I from the MaxGen Alert to MaxGen Warning stage.  MISO asserts that, after investigation, it took this action because stakeholders understood the need for longer lead resources to be deployed earlier in the Emergency Operating Procedures but requested that these resources be deployed during the EEA-Level 1 stage.  Thus, MISO asserts that the proposal is a just and reasonable resolution of stakeholder concerns.
MISO responds to ALLETE’s and IMEA’s concerns that the 30-minute response requirement for LMR-Type II is not just and reasonable by explaining that LMR-Type II is a committable reliability resource that must be capable of quickly reducing Demand when deployed during, or in anticipation of, an EEA-Level 2 declaration.  MISO asserts that, while some stakeholders, including ALLETE, questioned the need for a 30-minute response time in favor of a two-hour lead time, requiring LMR-Type II to be deployable within 30 minutes ensures that these resources are always available.  MISO adds that, because approximately half of EEA-Level 2 declarations have less than a one-hour lead time between the declaration and the start of the event, imposing a 90-minute or two-hour response time would be insufficient to ensure reliability.  Accordingly, MISO argues that ALLETE’s and IMEA’s protests should be disregarded.
In response to arguments from Advanced Energy and Voltus opposing the elimination of dual registration, MISO argues that these claims should be rejected as out of scope because MISO proposed eliminating the dual registration of EDRs in Docket No. ER25-2050-000.
Lastly, MISO states that it agrees with Midwest TDUs that the proposed Tariff revisions do not implement MISO’s intent to restrict the ability of resources to switch between Emergency and Non-Emergency participation by requiring a resource to wait three Planning Years after registering.  MISO explains that Midwest TDUs correctly point out that the three-year period was not intended to mean that a resource must participate for all three Planning Years, but instead that three consecutive Planning Years must pass before a resource can switch, regardless of the number of Auctions in which it participates in during that time.  MISO states that it will adjust the Tariff language to clarify this issue, if so directed by the Commission.
