Commission Determination
We find that MISO’s proposed reforms to demand-side resource participation options are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential as they establish clear performance expectations, improve operational flexibility, and provide a range of participation options to accommodate different types of demand-side resources.  In particular, we find that MISO’s proposal to incentivize different resources to be available for Demand reduction at different stages of deployment aligns resource commitments with system needs, thus leading to improved overall performance during Emergencies.  We note that the Commission has previously found just and reasonable MISO’s efforts to ensure that demand-side resources can contribute their registered load reduction capabilities during Emergency events, particularly given MISO’s increasing reliance on, and the historical underperformance of, demand-side resources.  For these reasons, we are unpersuaded by protesters’ arguments that MISO’s proposed participation options, if implemented, may unduly limit, exclude, or otherwise disincentivize demand-side resources from participating in MISO’s markets.  In response to claims by IMEA and OMS that MISO’s proposal may make demand response programs run by LSEs more burdensome, costly, and difficult to explain to participating resources, we find that MISO’s proposed range of participation options reasonably balances MISO’s operational needs with resources’ ability to participate in MISO’s markets depending on the type and operating characteristics of their resources and each market participant’s goals.
We similarly find that MISO’s proposal to eliminate dual registration of DRR-Type I and LMR is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  In accepting a separate MISO proposal to remove the ability for market participants to dual register as EDR and either DRR or LMR, the Commission found that, “despite MISO’s proposal to eliminate the opportunity for dual registration for EDR resources, [D]emand [R]esources continue to have the opportunity to participate in both MISO’s capacity and energy markets.”  In that proceeding, the Commission rejected the assertion that dual-registered resources would be left without a viable path to earn both capacity and energy payments, which is the same argument that Voltus and Advanced Energy raise in the instant proposal.  Thus, consistent with the Commission’s past findings, we find that MISO’s proposal to eliminate dual registration of DRR-Type I and LMR is just and reasonable because resources can continue to participate in both MISO’s capacity and energy markets through the DRR-Type I or DRR-Type II participation options.  Similarly, regarding Voltus’ concern with the burdensome nature of providing EPNode information for each facility underlying a DRR during enrollment, we note that MISO’s proposal does not add a new provision to, or otherwise modify an existing provision of, the Tariff to require such information.  We find, therefore, that this issue is beyond the scope of this proceeding.
Regarding Midwest TDUs’ argument that MISO’s proposal eliminates all options for DRR-Type I with notification time requirements longer than six hours to participate in both capacity and energy markets, we agree with MISO that Midwest TDUs’ concerns are misplaced because the existing Tariff does not permit resources with a notification time greater than six hours to register as a Demand Resource.  Regarding Midwest TDUs’ request that MISO should confirm that DRR-Type I is not subject to a must offer requirement, we note MISO’s clarification that the proposal does not include a Day-Ahead must offer requirement for DRR-Type I.
We agree with MISO that splitting LMRs into two types and requiring LMR-Type II to deploy within a 30-minute window will enable MISO to better respond to Emergencies.  We are unpersuaded by protesters’ arguments for extending the proposed 30-minute response time for LMR-Type II or, as ALLETE suggests, deploying long-lead LMR-Type I at the beginning of the MaxGen Warning stage while reserving short-lead LMR-Type I for deployment at the beginning of an EEA-Level 2 declaration.  Instead, we find that the proposed deployment order is just and reasonable because it balances MISO’s need to guarantee the effectiveness of using these resources during an Emergency with stakeholders’ preference for participation options that allow for deployment later in MISO’s Emergency Operating Procedures.  Further, MISO’s proposal reasonably balances MISO’s need to quickly respond to Emergencies while also accommodating different resources’ operational characteristics by providing a range of participation options.  Additionally, we agree with MISO that revising the definitions of LMR-Type I and LMR-Type II to accommodate multiple ownership structures, as proposed by AMP, is unnecessary because the proposed definitions allow for such variations.  Moreover, we note that the phrase “owned by a single [LSE], or an ARC” in the proposed LMR-Type I and LMR-Type II definitions is consistent with the currently effective definitions for DRR-Type I and DRR-Type II.
Finally, we agree with Midwest TDUs that the proposed Tariff revisions do not implement MISO’s stated intent to require a resource to wait three Planning Years after registering in the Auction before switching between Emergency and Non-Emergency participation.  In its answer, MISO states that, if directed by the Commission, it will adjust the Tariff language to clarify that three consecutive Planning Years must pass before a resource can switch, regardless of the number of Auctions in which it participates during that time.  Accordingly, we direct MISO to file, within 30 days of the date of this order, a compliance filing to incorporate into the Tariff language clarifying MISO’s stated intent to require a resource to wait three Planning Years after registering in the Auction before switching between Emergency and Non-Emergency participation.
Real-Time Availability, and Measurement and Verification
MISO’s Filing
Real-Time Availability
MISO explains that all demand-side resources are currently required to submit availability information and to keep such information updated at all times, except for de minimis changes, irrespective of whether a resource participates in MISO’s capacity market and/or energy markets.  MISO states, however, that it has identified three issues regarding the availability and visibility of resources under its existing accreditation process:  (1) dual registration makes it difficult to track whether each component of a dual-registered resource is meeting its obligations; (2) a significant number of LMRs never update their availability information, which causes operators to question resources’ true availabilities; and (3) the lack of meter data prevents MISO from validating offers.
In response to these issues, MISO proposes two changes:  (1) removing the dual registration option for DRRs and LMRs so that MISO can track the availability of every resource on an individual basis and accurately verify performance; and (2) collecting hourly meter data for Demand Resources for every hour of each Planning Year.  MISO states that having year-round access to resources’ meter data will improve visibility and operator confidence because MISO will be able to verify offers.  MISO explains that a resource that consistently overstates its Demand reduction capability, as shown through the submitted meter data, will be identified and, if necessary, referred to the IMM.
MISO proposes to collect five-minute meter data for any demand-side resource with a registered response time of one hour or less that has been issued either Setpoint Instructions or Scheduling Instructions to ensure that these resources are deployed in a manner consistent with their registration parameters.  MISO explains that hourly meter data is insufficient for these resources because, in certain situations where deployment instructions are issued in narrow timeframes, the response may not be verified within one hour.  According to MISO, the data collected over five-minute intervals will give MISO insight into the operational pattern of these resources, thus providing a greater understanding of their performance capabilities and assisting with identifying manipulative behaviors.  MISO also explains that, as periods of expected risks shift, the proposed meter data requirements will enable MISO to more fully track the performance of demand-side resources during off-peak conditions as well as during peak conditions, rather than only during peak load conditions under MISO’s current design.
Measurement and Verification
MISO further proposes to revise its Measurement and Verification procedures in Attachment TT of the Tariff by adding a new baseline, the statistical interval baseline, and formalizing the existing Firm Service Level baseline.  MISO explains that, under its proposal, Demand Resources will be able to choose from four defined types of Measurement and Verification methodologies:  (1) the existing calculated baseline; (2) the existing direct load control baseline; (3) the newly proposed statistical interval baseline; and (4) the newly codified Firm Service Level baseline.  MISO proposes to group the direct load control and statistical interval baselines, as well as the existing custom baseline, under a collective new term, Statistical Measurement and Verification.
MISO states that the proposed statistical interval baseline will be available for use by Demand Resources comprised of an aggregation of at least 100 components that all have hourly metered Demand data.  MISO explains that the statistical interval baseline is a sampling methodology that reduces the meter submission requirements for large aggregations that all have hourly metered Demand data and wish to use a Measurement and Verification approach similar to that of the calculated baseline.  MISO also proposes to add the Firm Service Level baseline into Attachment TT, which obligates a Demand Resource to reduce Demand to or below the Firm Service Level, regardless of the amount of Demand being consumed.  Additionally, MISO proposes to exclude aggregations from using the Firm Service Level baseline because, according to MISO, there is no way to ensure that each component of an aggregation can achieve the required level of Demand reduction.
MISO explains that, under its proposal, DRRs may use any baseline except for the Firm Service Level baseline because, rather than providing a mechanism to measure how much Demand reduction occurred, the Firm Service Level baseline measures only whether Demand was reduced to a specific point.  MISO explains that this exemption is necessary because DRRs are compensated for Demand reduction that occurs due to a MISO instruction, and that, without the ability to compare Demand to previous days, it is impossible for MISO to determine whether the Demand reduction would have otherwise occurred absent MISO instruction.  In contrast, MISO states that LMRs are reliability resources that are not compensated via LMP, and, as such, they may use any measurement and verification baseline defined in Attachment TT.
Responsive Pleadings
Comments in Support
COMPP and DTE Electric contend that MISO’s proposed meter data requirements will help protect against market manipulation and gaming schemes.  DTE Electric supports MISO’s proposal to collect year-round meter data.  COMPP asserts that collecting hourly meter data will allow MISO to understand the availability of demand-side resources and ensure that they are properly deployed and accredited. 
COMPP contends that the use of multiple baselines, rather than relying on event-based or hypothetical performance scenarios, ties accreditation to the real-world, observed behavior of resources, thus enhancing the credibility of resources’ contributions and helping to prevent inflated or inconsistent capacity values.  Similarly, DTE Electric agrees with MISO that adding the Firm Service Level baseline and the statistical interval baseline to Attachment TT will remove ambiguity related to the calculation of resources’ Measurement and Verification and allow for more robust accreditation.
Protests
Advanced Energy argues that MISO’s proposal to collect meter data for every hour of the Planning Year, and for resources with less than a one-hour response time to provide five-minute interval data, is too strict.  Advanced Energy asserts that, while it understands the need to have greater visibility into performance capabilities, the five-minute requirement for resources with a response time of less than one hour may be overly restrictive because it could preclude resources from participating, particularly those with longer lead times closer to one hour.  Moreover, Advanced Energy claims that utility data is often reported in 15-minute intervals, rather than the five-minute interval that MISO proposes, which would require market participants to install separate metering to provide this additional granularity.  Advanced Energy argues that, if the equipment is too cost-prohibitive to install, there is a risk that resources would not be able to comply, thus making them unable to participate.  Therefore, Advanced Energy requests that the Commission direct MISO to remove the five-minute meter data requirement.
Entergy Services argues that categorically excluding aggregated resources from using the Firm Service Level baseline seems arbitrary and may lead to limitations in resource participation.  Entergy Services claims that MISO cites the inability to measure each component’s performance as justification for excluding aggregated resources from using the Firm Service Level baseline.  Entergy Services notes, however, that the statistical interval baseline for aggregated Demand Resources of 100 components or more requires a calculation based on a sample of the component resources’ performance.  Entergy Services claims that, because not all aggregated resources meet the 100-component threshold to use the statistical interval baseline, some of these resources may need to use a calculated baseline methodology in order to participate.  Thus, Entergy Services contends that, if the Firm Service Level baseline is calculated at the aggregated level, it may be reasonable to calculate performance at the total level as well.
Voltus similarly argues that, from a reliability perspective, it is irrelevant whether each individual component of an aggregation curtails to its specific Firm Service Level because MISO is receiving the aggregate response that it requires if the aggregation, as a whole, has load less than or equal to its registered Firm Service Level.  Voltus asserts that one of the key values of aggregated demand response is that the collective curtailment behavior of large volumes of facilities is much more predictable and reliable than the curtailment behavior of any individual facility.  Voltus contends that, in any large aggregation, underperformance and overperformance are expected and planned for so that each customer is not required to meet every requirement.  In turn, according to Voltus, this leads to an increased statistical predictability of curtailment at higher volumes of facilities that results in more accurate enrollment volumes and improved performance and predictability for MISO.  Although Voltus asserts that it expects every individual facility to be ready and willing to curtail if enrolled as an LMR, Voltus argues that MISO’s proposal ignores the reality that an aggregation provides a more reliable path to predicting and managing instances of resource underperformance and would discriminate against an individual resource that cannot meet MISO’s 100 kV minimum size requirement.  Voltus asserts that other RTOs/ISOs allow aggregations to use a Firm Service Level baseline methodology, and, as such, Voltus requests that the Commission direct MISO to eliminate its proposed prohibition against aggregated resources from using the Firm Service Level baseline.
Voltus further asserts that prohibiting aggregations from using the Firm Service Level baseline, as revised in Attachment TT, was neither publicly discussed nor vetted with stakeholders.  Voltus argues that many LMRs favor and select the Firm Service Level baseline as their Measurement and Verification methodology, and will continue to do so, because curtailing all non-essential load is more direct and less burdensome than calculating the exact load reduction value that these resources can provide under alternative baseline methodologies.  Voltus contends that, rather than entirely removing this Measurement and Verification option for aggregations, MISO should develop a location-based registration and approval process for LMRs—which Voltus asserts that it has urged MISO to develop for years—to provide sufficient visibility into each individual location’s registered Firm Service Level.  Moreover, Voltus asserts that MISO could review the deployment performance of each individual component in an LMR aggregation by reviewing the meter data that MISO proposes to collect.
DTE Electric states that, while it supports MISO’s proposal, more work is necessary to increase the level of standardization, transparency, and enforcement across all LMR-related processes to ensure consistency and performance among all participants in MISO’s markets.  Specifically, DTE Electric asserts that MISO should continue working with stakeholders to determine a method to track which customers and meters roll up to each LMR registration, which can be made up of hundreds to thousands of individual meters.  DTE Electric argues that it is critical to ensure that poor performing customer meters, which either fail tests and are disqualified from participation in the Auction, or lower accreditation of an entire LMR, are not removed from their initial registration group and included in another LMR registration to avoid the consequences of poor performance.  DTE Electric claims that, without this type of tracking, MISO cannot determine if an LMR registration includes customer meters that were previously barred from participating in the Auction due to poor performance.
Answers
MISO Answer
In response to Advanced Energy’s argument that the five-minute meter data requirement for resources with a notification time of less than one hour is too strict and could reduce participation from resources with lead times closer to one hour, MISO argues that this proposed requirement ensures that resources provide notice reflective of their ability to perform so that MISO can deploy such resources in the appropriate order.  MISO explains that it intends to deploy resources in order of decreasing notification time (i.e., six-hour resources will be deployed more frequently than two-hour resources), and that, by having the flexibility to deploy resources closer to when an Emergency begins, there is greater certainty as to whether the resources are truly needed.  MISO notes, however, that it recently learned that this can incentivize market participants to input lower notification times to minimize their probability of deployment.  Consequently, MISO explains that requiring five-minute interval data for resources submitting a notification time under one hour ensures that these resources are submitting notification times reflective of their ability to perform.
MISO further argues that five-minute interval data is needed because, without it, a resource will not have its performance verified for at least one hour after deployment.  MISO explains, for example, that a resource with a one-hour notification time could take up to one hour and 45 minutes to deploy while still appearing to have met its obligations.  MISO notes that, in contrast, under the proposed five-minute meter data requirement, a resource with a 30-minute notification time would only have 35 minutes before being identified as failing to perform, which ensures that only resources that can truly perform submit notification times commensurate with this deployment time.  
MISO also argues that, without five-minute interval data, long-interval metering requirements would enable market participants that could not respond within 30 minutes to register resources as LMR-Type II.  MISO claims that this could result in the number of resources claiming a short-lead time increasing, which would crowd out assets that have invested in the technologies and processes that provide for a rapid response due to the increased probability that truly flexible resources would be deployed more frequently than intended.  Additionally, MISO explains that resources that are unable to provide five-minute interval data, or prefer not to, simply need to submit longer notification times of at least one hour.  While MISO acknowledges that such resources would not be permitted to participate as LMR-Type II, MISO reiterates that this participation option is explicitly designed for resources with high reliability and availability, and, moreover, that part of meeting this requirement is installing the equipment necessary to perform and demonstrate such performance.
In response to Entergy Services’ and Voltus’ arguments that prohibiting aggregations from using the Firm Service Level baseline is arbitrary and unreasonable, MISO asserts that these claims lack merit.  In particular, MISO disputes the assertions that the exclusion would create a barrier to participation for small resources.  MISO argues that this is untrue because, rather than requiring aggregations that currently use the Firm Service Level to disaggregate, MISO is instead requiring these aggregations to use a different Measurement and Verification methodology so that Demand reduction is required at the same level whether or not resources are aggregated.  MISO further disputes Voltus’ reliance on the fact that other RTOs/ISOs permit aggregations to use the Firm Service Level baseline because, according to MISO, Voltus’ argument lacks merit and distorts the applicable legal standard under section 205.
MISO states that it considered removing the Firm Service Level methodology entirely, but, after stakeholder feedback, MISO retained the methodology with certain restrictions.  MISO explains that the reason to exclude aggregations from the Firm Service Level baseline is rooted in the operation of the baseline and how it interacts with an aggregation.  To this point, MISO asserts that:  (1) the overperformance of one resource may make up for the underperformance of another resource; and (2) the Firm Service Level baseline measures the level to which a resource reduces Demand, not by how much a resource reduces Demand.  MISO argues that these two factors allow aggregations using the Firm Service Level baseline to significantly reduce the probability of reducing Demand while still receiving the same payments as if they were individually registered.
MISO states that the purpose of the Firm Service Level is to set a level of consumption by a resource that must always be maintained.  MISO explains that overperformance of a resource using the Firm Service Level baseline means that the resource has dropped below the point stated by the market participant as always needing to be consumed, which leads to questions regarding the validity of the Firm Service Level.  While MISO notes that 1 MW of underperformance is permitted for each MW of overperformance, MISO argues that, if enough resources are overperforming (i.e., consuming less than their Firm Service Level), then any resource operating above the Firm Service Level is not required to curtail because the aggregation is meeting its obligations.  Therefore, MISO argues that, despite sending out a Scheduling Instruction, no load is curtailed in that scenario because the resource is meeting its performance obligations, which means that resources are being compensated for doing nothing.
MISO states that it performed a Monte Carlo analysis to demonstrate how aggregations can be structured to significantly lower the possibility of having to curtail load while still receiving full payment and accreditation.  MISO asserts that, based on this analysis, an aggregation registering its components individually is more likely to be required to curtail load and provide needed system relief than an aggregation using the Firm Service Level baseline.  In particular, MISO notes that, under a scenario in which three 10 MW components are registered separately with equivalent Firm Service Levels of 2.5 MW, at least one of the three components would need to be deployed approximately 93% of the time.  MISO asserts, however, that, if these same three components are registered as an aggregation, the probability that at least one component would need to be deployed would be approximately 79%, resulting in the probability for required action to decrease by approximately 15% despite receiving the same compensation.  MISO states that, if this same aggregation uses the calculated baseline, where the market participant submits the total Demand reduction achievable for each component based on how far above its Firm Service Level the resource is operating, MISO could expect an identical amount of Demand reduction whether registered in aggregation or individually.  Additionally, MISO asserts that market participants may register any desired Firm Service Level, and, because MISO has no means to verify whether the registered Firm Service Level represents a true limit, a market participant could dramatically impact the probability of being deployed by changing the Firm Service Level of the aggregated resources.
Thus, MISO argues that, based on the Monte Carlo analysis, only the Firm Service Level baseline provides a mechanism for an aggregation to do nothing while meeting its performance obligations.  Moreover, MISO asserts that it is inappropriate to make capacity payments to resources that do not need to respond to Emergencies, particularly as MISO’s proposal is intended to ensure that accreditation reflects how often demand-side resources respond to Emergencies and the level at which they perform.  MISO contends, therefore, that requiring these resources to use a different Measurement and Verification baseline, or register individually, ensures that some level of performance is required.
Commission Determination
We find that the proposed hourly meter data requirement for DRRs and LMRs is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential because hourly meter data will provide MISO with more information regarding resources’ actual performance capabilities, thus allowing MISO to have greater visibility of available demand-side resources during times of high system risk.  Further, we agree that the proposed meter data requirement will help ensure that a resource’s accreditation is aligned with its availability and performance during times of high system risk, consistent with the DLOL accreditation methodology.
We find that Advanced Energy’s concerns regarding the five-minute interval meter data requirement are unfounded for two reasons.  First, we find that MISO has sufficiently supported its proposal to collect five-minute meter interval data for resources with faster response times.  Namely, we agree with MISO that five-minute meter interval data will hold such resources accountable for performing consistent with their stated capabilities.  Second, resources are not obligated to register with a notification time of less than one hour; MISO only requires five-minute meter data for those resources that voluntarily commit to rapidly respond to MISO instructions.  Although producing more granular meter data may be more costly and burdensome for market participants due to, among other things, the potential need to install new meters, we find that MISO reasonably balances its need for visibility to ensure reliability against any resulting cost burden for market participants.
Additionally, we find that MISO’s proposed changes to its Measurement and Verification procedures are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential because these proposed changes will help ensure that resources’ load reduction capabilities are not overstated as well as remove ambiguity related to how demand-side resources’ performance is measured.  Regarding revisions to the Measurement and Verification consumption baselines in Attachment TT, we find that the proposed addition of the statistical interval baseline will provide more effective Measurement and Verification options for larger aggregations in addition to the direct load control baseline.  Although MISO proposes to exclude aggregations of resources from using the Firm Service Level baseline, as explained below, we find that aggregations would retain several options, including the direct load control and statistical interval baselines, when considering the most effective way to accurately measure and verify their load reduction capabilities, thus mitigating concerns regarding participation options available to aggregations.
We also find that MISO’s proposal to formally incorporate the Firm Service Level baseline into Attachment TT is just and reasonable because it will clearly define and standardize the performance expectations for resources using this baseline, thus providing greater clarity for both MISO and market participants.  We disagree with Voltus and Entergy Services that MISO’s exclusion of aggregations from using the Firm Service Level baseline is unreasonable or arbitrary, as we find that MISO has adequately supported its proposal.  Specifically, we agree with MISO that individual components of an aggregation using the Firm Service Level baseline to measure their performance are less likely to need to perform (i.e., to curtail load) in response to MISO instructions due to the unique performance obligation of the Firm Service Level baseline that permits one over-performing component to make up for an under-performing component in the same aggregation, thus disincentivizing the very performance for which these resources are compensated.  Therefore, we find that it is reasonable to prohibit aggregations from choosing this baseline to ensure that at least some degree of actual performance is required from all demand-side resources, regardless of their registered Measurement and Verification baseline methodology.
We need not address the alternative proposals raised by Voltus and DTE Electric because we find, as discussed above, that MISO’s proposed reforms to Measurement and Verification, and real-time availability, are just and reasonable.  Accordingly, we decline Voltus’ requests that the Commission require that MISO:  (1) align its approach for the Measurement and Verification of aggregations with PJM, ERCOT, or NYISO; and (2) develop a location-based registration and approval process for LMRs.  We similarly decline DTE Electric’s request that the Commission direct MISO to develop a method to track customer accounts and meter numbers to prevent repeat registrations of poor performers.
Accreditation
MISO states that it currently accredits demand-side resources based on SAC values determined according to Module E-1 and Schedule 53 of the Tariff, as well as the MISO Resource Adequacy Business Practices Manual (Resource Adequacy BPM), but that this framework has faced several key issues related to resource availability, performance variability, and misalignment with system needs.  In particular, MISO explains that its current framework does not always accurately reflect demand-side resources’ true reliability contributions during hours of highest system risk, which leads to the over-accreditation of resources that may not be fully available when needed.  MISO further explains that its current accreditation process has struggled to account for changing system conditions and real-world performance, which can result in higher reliability risks by over accrediting resources that may not be fully available when needed, thereby driving out reliable resources.
MISO asserts that updating the accreditation of demand-side resources and Emergency supply-side resources to be based on the capability of resources when they are most needed ensures that accreditation is based on availability and performance during times of highest system risk, and, further, aligns with the DLOL methodology used for Schedule 53A Resources.  In proposing reforms related to accreditation, MISO focuses on four components:  (1) the choice of accreditation hours; (2) assigning certain resources to Resource Classes; (3) the application of an availability cap for DRR-Type I and LMRs; and (4) a lookback period to gauge historical performance.
Accreditation Hours and Performance Therein
MISO’s Filing
Selection of Hours
MISO states that the selection of hours used to accredit each resource type is determined by a resource’s obligations to be available and the hours during which the resource may be deployed.  MISO explains that Schedule 53A Resources and DRR-Type II are obligated to be available during all hours because these resources may be committed at any time; therefore, it is appropriate to use all hours when accrediting these resources.  MISO similarly states that, while Non-Emergency BTMG resources have no obligation to be available to respond to MISO instructions, it is appropriate to accredit these resources during all hours of a Season because they provide capacity to the MISO system during all hours they operate.  MISO contends that, in contrast, it is appropriate to accredit DRR-Type I and LMRs only during the hours when they are likely to be deployed because these resources may only be deployed during Emergency conditions.  MISO proposes, therefore, to accredit demand response and Emergency supply-side resources using Capacity At Risk Hours and RA Hours during each Season, pursuant to newly proposed Schedule 53B.
MISO states that the periods of highest system risk are defined as either Capacity At Risk Hours or RA Hours.  MISO explains that a Capacity At Risk Hour, a newly defined term, is an hour during which MISO has made a capacity advisory, MaxGen Alert, MaxGen Warning, or MaxGen Event declaration.  MISO further explains that RA Hours represent the periods of highest risk and greatest need during a Season and throughout the year, which include hours during MaxGen Events.  MISO states that RA Hours may occur at any time, but that there are certain daily patterns.  MISO explains that these values are not expected to shift dramatically from one year to the next, though they may shift over time.  Further, MISO notes that all Capacity At Risk Hours that occur during a MaxGen Alert declaration or higher will also be RA Hours, and that while this creates overlap, RA Hours and Capacity At Risk Hours are two distinct concepts.
MISO states that it proposes to accredit demand response and Emergency supply-side resources during RA Hours and Capacity At Risk Hours to ensure that resources are accredited during times they may be used.  MISO explains that using RA Hours stabilizes the accreditation of resources using hours reflective of the expected time of use of these resources.  MISO further explains that using both RA Hours and Capacity At Risk Hours ensures that accreditation naturally adjusts as system risks shift off of Summer and seasonal peaks, which MISO contends is not possible under its current accreditation framework.
Capability and Seasonal Capability
MISO proposes a new term, Capability, to represent the amount of Demand reduction that a demand-side resource can provide or has provided.  MISO states that the Capability value, which is analogous to an Offer from a Schedule 53A Resource, is submitted by market participants and may be updated in real-time, subject to restrictions based on the lead-time of the resource.  MISO states that it will cap the Capability of a demand-side resource by the resource’s Generation Verification Test Capacity or Capacity Rating, as applicable.  MISO explains that a resource would be available for deployment during those hours when the resource’s Capability is above zero.

MISO proposes to calculate Capability for resources during normal operations (i.e., when MISO has not issued a Setpoint Instruction or a Scheduling Instruction).  MISO explains that there are four unique classifications for determining the Capability of resources participating as DRR-Type I or LMR, which are based on the different Attachment TT-defined Measurement and Verification baselines:  (1) BTMG; (2) calculated baseline; (3) Statistical Measurement and Verification; and (4) Firm Service Level.  The Capability of BTMG is the sum of the metered output and the Capacity Availability, submitted in real-time by the market participant, with this sum capped at the Generation Verification Test Capacity of the resource.  The Capability of a Demand Resource using the calculated baseline is the minimum of:  (1) the meter value submitted by the market participant after the fact for that hour; (2) the real-time submitted Capacity Availability; or (3) the registered Capacity Rating.  The Capability of a Demand Resource using a Statistical Measurement and Verification methodology is the minimum of:  (1) the Capacity Availability submitted in real-time by the market participant; (2) the Load Curve submitted by the Market Participant at registration; or (3) the registered Capacity Rating.  The Capability of a Demand Resource using a Firm Service Level baseline is:  (1) equal to Demand less Firm Service Level if Demand is more than the Firm Service Level; (2) zero if the resource is consuming Demand at or below the Firm Service Level during an RA Hour that is not a Capacity At Risk Hour; or (3) the Seasonal Capability, a new term described below, if the resource is consuming Demand at or below the Firm Service Level during a Capacity At Risk Hour.
MISO explains that its proposed new term, Seasonal Capability, indicates what a resource using the Firm Service Level baseline would have consumed had it not been deployed.  MISO states that this is necessary because there is no baseline to estimate what the resource would be doing but for the MISO instruction.  Additionally, MISO asserts that Seasonal Capability provides a strong incentive to a resource to remain at or below its Firm Service Level during Capacity At Risk Hours.
MISO explains that, to determine Seasonal Capability, MISO distinguishes between Business Days and non-Business Days.  MISO proposes that, for each hour of the Business Days within each Season, Seasonal Capability will be determined using the average of the 15 hours with a resource’s highest Demand less the Firm Service Level.  MISO further proposes that, for each hour of the non-Business Days within each Season, Seasonal Capability will be calculated using the average of the six hours with a resource’s highest Demand less the Firm Service Level.  MISO explains that these hours represent approximately the top 25% of Demand being consumed, calculated separately for each hour of the day, and that MISO will calculate unique values for Business Days and non-Business Days to account for any differences in the operations of Demand Resources that occur on a Business Day compared to those that occur on a non-Business Day.
Under MISO’s proposal, Demand Resources that fully meet a Setpoint Instruction or Scheduling Instruction will receive Capability in the following manner:  (1) for resources using a Statistical Measurement and Verification methodology or a calculated baseline, Capability will equal the Capability for the first hour of the MISO instruction; and (2) for resources using the Firm Service Level baseline, Capability will equal the resource’s Seasonal Capability for the hour.  MISO proposes to apply this Capability value to:  (1) each hour preceding the MISO instruction, capped at the registered notification time of the resource; (2) for each hour of the MISO instruction; and (3) for one hour after the MISO instruction.
Capacity Availability, Capacity Availability Thresholds, and Capability Adjustments
MISO proposes a new term, Capacity Availability, to indicate how much energy a Demand Resource has made available in real-time, whether participating as a DRR or LMR.  MISO explains that hourly Capacity Availability values are capped at the registered Load Curve or submitted meter data.  MISO explains that Capacity Availability is necessary because DRR-Type I and LMRs are not obligated to be available for all Emergencies.
For any resource using the Firm Service Level baseline, MISO further proposes to modify that resource’s Capability when its Demand is above the Firm Service Level and its Capacity Availability is above or below certain Capacity Availability Thresholds.  MISO explains that it has leveraged existing language regarding performance Tolerance Bands, as defined in the Tariff, to develop the Capacity Availability Thresholds.  Specifically, MISO proposes that the Excessive Capacity Availability Threshold is equal to 112% of the difference between the amount of Demand that is metered and the Firm Service Level, and that, when Capacity Availability is above the Excessive Capacity Availability Threshold, a resource’s Capability will be reduced by the difference between the Capacity Availability and the Excessive Capacity Availability Threshold, but the reduction will never result in a Capability value less than zero.  MISO further proposes for the Deficient Capacity Availability Threshold to be equal to 88% of the difference between the amount of Demand that is metered and the Firm Service Level, and that, when Capacity Availability is below the Deficient Capacity Availability Threshold, a resource’s Capability will be equal to the submitted Capacity Availability.  MISO states that it developed the Capacity Availability Thresholds based on the actual response that a resource is required to provide, and that if a market participant has made available to MISO an amount within the Capacity Availability Thresholds, the availability information will be considered accurate.  
MISO explains that the Capacity Availability Thresholds and performance Tolerance Bands incentivize market participants to provide accurate information such that, if a resource does not perform to the level of its stated Capacity Availability, the market participant faces penalties.  MISO states that the proposed Tariff revisions confirm that LMR performance will be subject to Measurement & Verification pursuant to Attachment TT and penalties pursuant to section 69A.3.9.
Seasonal Emergency Hour Deficiency
MISO states that, when there are fewer than a combined 65 Capacity At Risk Hours and RA Hours in a Season, a Seasonal Emergency Hour Deficiency exists.  MISO proposes to incorporate a Seasonal Emergency Hour Deficiency when accrediting behind the meter generation resources by using the same methodology that MISO applies to Schedule 53A Resources (i.e., for each deficient hour, the missing value is calculated as the Resource Class-level UCAP as a percentage of the corresponding Resource Class-level Installed Capacity (ICAP), multiplied by the resource’s ICAP).  MISO further proposes to incorporate a Seasonal Emergency Hour Deficiency when accrediting Demand Resources by taking the product of the Seasonal Emergency Hour Deficiency and one of the following:  (1) the registered Capacity Rating for resources using a calculated baseline or a custom baseline; (2) the Load Curve for resources using a Statistical Measurement and Verification methodology; or (3) the average of all Seasonal Capability values in a Season for resources using the Firm Service Level baseline.
Self Scheduling
MISO proposes to change Demand Resources’ ability to Self Schedule, thus affecting the hours during which a resource is considered available for deployment.  MISO explains that, while behind the meter generation resources that Self Schedule will always receive accreditation for the Self Schedule, Demand Resources may only receive accreditation when Self Scheduled during a Capacity At Risk Hour and, further, only if:  (1) a Demand Resource using a calculated baseline has Self Scheduled to the full registered Capacity Rating; (2) a Demand Resource using a Statistical Measurement and Verification methodology has Self Scheduled to the appropriate Load Curve value, representing the estimated Capability of the Demand Resource given the conditions prevalent at that hour; or (3) a Demand Resource using a Firm Service Level has Self Scheduled to or below the Firm Service Level.  MISO further proposes to disallow resources from self-scheduling to a partial amount because a gaming opportunity would otherwise be available.
Planned Outage Exemptions
Under MISO’s proposal, BTMG resources would be subject to non-performance penalties for any hours in which the resources are unavailable to respond to MISO instructions, including for planned outages, except due to force majeure.  Similarly, MISO proposes to exclude Non-Emergency BTMG from the planned outage exemptions that are available to Schedule 53A Resources.
MISO explains that behind the meter generation resources may desire to participate in outage coordination, but the benefits of accreditation come with responsibilities that behind the meter generation resources either cannot or do not have.  In particular, MISO states that, unlike behind the meter generation resources, Generation Resources are required to participate in Generator Interconnection Studies and Generator Interconnection Agreements, to obtain Transmission Service, and are subject to economic and physical withholding provisions, among other requirements.  MISO asserts, therefore, that it would be unjust and unreasonable to permit behind the meter generation resources to participate in potentially beneficial aspects without also incurring the additional costs and obligations associated with those benefits.
Moreover, MISO states that, while it is responsible for coordinating with Generator Owners, as appropriate, to schedule maintenance on Generation Resources, MISO has no authority to reschedule outages of behind the meter generation resources.  MISO states, therefore, that treating behind the meter generation resources in a comparable manner as Generation Resources for outage coordination begins to blur the line between resources subject to MISO control and resources that are not.  MISO further states that, although behind the meter generation resources are treated differently with regard to outage coordination, they are not being unduly discriminated against because they may elect to participate as Generation Resources after undertaking the necessary costs and studies required of such resources.

Answers
MISO Answer
MISO asserts that IMEA’s concerns that the use of Capacity At Risk Hours and RA Hours to accredit LMRs breaks with MISO’s current resource adequacy construct are unfounded.  MISO explains that it generally accredits resources across all hours of the year, with greater weight placed on RA Hours, but that it would be inappropriate to accredit LMRs across all hours of the year because these resources are not expected or required to perform across the whole year.  MISO explains that it initially believed that it would be appropriate to accredit LMRs only during Capacity At Risk Hours, which would accredit these resources when there is an increased chance of use, but included RA Hours at the request of stakeholders because RA Hours are highly correlated with the times that DRR-Type I and LMRs are expected to be needed.  MISO further explains that including RA Hours helps stabilize accreditation values and ensures that an accurate signal is sent regarding the performance capabilities of resources in each Season.  Therefore, MISO asserts that, while it proposes to use a different set of hours to accredit LMRs than those used for Generation Resources, doing so merely adjusts MISO’s resource adequacy construct to accommodate the unique operating characteristics of certain resources.
Additionally, MISO explains that, because Emergencies may escalate quickly and Capacity At Risk Hours are known in real-time, market participants gain additional hours of accreditation during periods in which the likelihood of deployment has increased and, moreover, receive accreditation during hours that are known in real-time.  MISO contends that market participants will benefit by having improved knowledge of when they will be accredited and will receive accreditation during hours in which they have voluntarily curtailed Demand.  Further, MISO states that it expects reliability benefits through improved confidence in the amount of LMRs available for deployment and by ensuring that this information is submitted in a timely manner.  Thus, MISO argues that, in contrast to IMEA’s suggestion, the use of Capacity At Risk Hours is appropriate for resources that are required to perform only during Emergencies.
In response to concerns from protesters regarding LSE Reserve Requirements allocations, MISO reiterates that aligning the accreditation of demand-side resources with their availability and performance during times of highest system risk is appropriately prioritized before addressing LSE Reserve Requirements.  MISO explains that it has begun discussions with stakeholders to align LSE Reserve Requirements allocations with the DLOL-based accreditation methodology, but that additional time is needed for evaluation and design before proposing such reforms.  MISO argues that, because commenters have not sufficiently justified postponing MISO’s proposal in favor of changes to the Reserve Requirements, the Commission should reject such protests and allow MISO to continue the stakeholder process.  Additionally, in response to assertions from ALLETE about the complexity of the instant proposal, MISO argues that this complexity is not inherently problematic because MISO’s proposal accommodates the competing needs of both MISO and its stakeholders.
Regarding Voltus’ concern that the proposed cap at the enrolled Capacity Rating does not incentivize maximum resource availability, MISO asserts that a resource may never receive greater accreditation than its maximum registered Demand reduction ability, but, if there is a mid-Season increase in capabilities, market participants may use the Demand Resource Test Deferral, which MISO proposes to adjust in a separate filing, to permit increases prior to a Season rather than increases prior to the Planning Year.
In response to Midwest TDUs’ arguments that the Capability adjustment is unduly discriminatory towards resources using the Firm Service Level baseline, MISO contends that Midwest TDUs fail to appreciate that a resource using the Firm Service Level baseline will fully meet its performance obligation if it meets its Firm Service Level regardless of the amount of reduction it provides.  Additionally, MISO asserts that a resource not using the Firm Service Level baseline must reduce its Demand to be within 12% of the submitted availability, and, because all resources have requirements regarding the accuracy of their submitted availability, Firm Service Level resources are not being discriminated against.  MISO argues that the requirement is simply being adjusted to facilitate the fundamental differences between the Firm Service Level baseline and other baselines.  According to MISO, it needs to further incentivize resources to update their reduction availability; therefore, MISO is adopting stricter rules to ensure that resources are complying with the Tariff as not all resources submit accurate availability information.
In response to Midwest TDUs’ assertion that the proposed Tariff language produces one 24-hour set of Seasonal Capability values for Business Days and one 24-hour set of Seasonal Capability values for non-Business Days, MISO states that it appreciates Midwest TDUs’ concerns.  MISO states that, if so ordered by the Commission, MISO will submit clarifications to backfill Seasonal Emergency Hour Deficiencies for Demand Resources that use the Firm Service Level baseline using only Business Days in the determination.
In response to assertions that MISO should afford resources more than one hour to return to business as usual following a MISO instruction, MISO argues that such claims miss the mark.  MISO states that it initially considered providing no additional accreditation after a deployment, but after stakeholders raised concerns with reduced accreditation when returning to normal operations, MISO responded by providing an additional hour.  Thus, MISO asserts that the proposed one-hour period balances MISO’s interest in resources voluntarily curtailing with market participants’ desire to improve their accreditation, and that balancing these competing considerations evidences MISO’s commitment to the stakeholder process rather than rendering the instant proposal unjust and unreasonable.  MISO adds that market participants concerned about accreditation after a deployment during an extraordinary Event (e.g., Winter Storm Uri) may self-curtail and receive accreditation for deploying.
In response to Steel Producers’ arguments against MISO’s proposed treatment of self-scheduling, MISO explains that the proposed reforms are to prevent fraud and abuse.  MISO argues that these concerns are not theoretical, as market participants have previously used self-scheduling to manipulate their Measurement and Verification baseline to artificially inflate their resources’ potential capability.  Thus, MISO explains that its proposal ensures that resources are not self-scheduling to a smaller amount to meet their obligations while receiving accreditation as a larger resource.  MISO states, however, that it recognizes that there is a legitimate purpose to self-scheduling during Capacity At Risk Hours, and, as such, MISO proposes to allow market participants to Self Schedule during these hours.
In response to BTMG Utilities’ argument that MISO’s proposal to only excuse non-performance of behind the meter generation resources due to force majeure would not allow for necessary preventive maintenance during planned outages, MISO asserts that removing the maintenance exemption addresses the reliability risk posed by resources claiming availability that are not, in fact, available.  MISO argues that behind the meter generation resources are Emergency resources that provide a critical reliability function and that, when such resources are unavailable, in many instances the load they serve must be served by the grid, adding to tight system conditions.  MISO emphasizes that a resource that states it is available when it is not harms reliability because operators believe there are more MWs available for deployment than truly exist.  MISO argues, therefore, that it is inappropriate to permit maintenance as a reason to not be available.
Further, MISO claims that, under the design suggested by BTMG Utilities where Scheduling Instructions in Demand Side Resource Interface would be based upon reported availability, operators issuing such instructions would be forced to make decisions based on their opinions about whether or not a resource was on outage.  As a result, MISO contends that a behind the meter generation resource could fail to update its availability and be confident that it would not face any penalties or reduced accreditation if it does not perform.  Moreover, MISO asserts that current information submitted to the Demand Side Resource Interface indicates that 40%-50% of all thermal behind the meter generation resources never update their availability, demonstrating that this is a current problem.
Additionally, MISO rebuts arguments from protesters that the absence of planned outage exemptions, including for behind the meter generation resources, is unjust and unreasonable because:  (1) behind the meter generation resources and Generation Resources are not similarly situated as Generation Resources must participate in outage coordination with MISO while behind the meter generation resources are not subject to this requirement; (2) behind the meter generation resources voluntarily participate as demand-side resources, which is a privilege not shared by Generation Resources, and therefore MISO is not discriminating against behind the meter generation resources as they have elected a participation option that does not permit planned outage exemptions; and (3) MISO lacks the ability to determine an adequate maintenance margin for behind the meter generation resources because, unlike Generation Resources, there is no requirement for behind the meter generation resources to provide telemetry, which limits MISO’s real-time visibility into the amount of behind the meter generation that is operating.
However, MISO states that it understands protesters’ concerns and therefore intends to propose Tariff language in a future filing that would allow a market participant to replace a specific LMR due to an outage with sufficient notice such that, when replaced, the LMR would not be subject to the availability cap.  MISO explains that, if accepted, this proposal should address the concern that a behind the meter generator resource would lose all accreditation while on a planned outage by providing market participants with a mechanism to maintain the same level of reliability as if that behind the meter generator resource was still in service.
Additional Answers

Midwest TDUs argue, therefore, that a potential future limited exemption from only the availability cap fails to address concerns related to the blanket exclusion of planned outage exemptions for behind the meter generation resources.

BTMG Utilities contend that the visibility and coordination of ordinary planned outages do not relate to the generating capability of a unit, yet behind the meter generation resources would be deprived of the option to engage in maintenance without risking accreditation. BTMG Utilities counter that behind the meter generation resources are generators just like Generation Resources.  Moreover, BTMG Utilities argue that any proposal that removes a generator’s ability to go offline for maintenance is not just and reasonable.
