Commission Determination
We find that MISO’s proposed reforms related to accreditation hours are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential, subject to condition, as discussed below.
We find that the use of RA Hours and Capacity At Risk Hours to accredit demand-side resources and AME Resources is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential because there are substantial similarities between proposed Schedule 53B and the Commission-approved DLOL methodology provided for in Schedule 53A.  As a result, MISO’s proposal will accredit resources based on their actual contributions to reliability and resource adequacy.  Similar to Schedule 53A, Schedule 53B would use RA Hours, in part, to accredit resources based on their availability during times of highest system risk.  Although MISO proposes certain modifications that distinguish proposed Schedule 53B from Schedule 53A, most notably the introduction of Capacity At Risk Hours, we believe that such modifications are just and reasonable because, where there are differences, such changes account for the operating characteristics and performance obligations that differentiate demand-side resources from supply-side resources.
Regarding concerns about the impact of MISO’s proposal on LSE Reserve Requirements, we find that, while there is a long-term need to ensure that both LSE Reserve Requirements and the accreditation of demand-side resources that are used to meet LSE Reserve Requirements are based on times of highest system risk, the lack of such alignment in MISO’s proposal does not render it unjust and unreasonable for two reasons.  First, we agree with MISO that reforms to demand-side resource accreditation should be implemented now to align with the accreditation of Generation Resources using the DLOL methodology.  Second, the instant proposal does not change the determination of LSE Reserve Requirements pursuant to section 68A.7 of the Tariff.  When considering MISO’s DLOL methodology, the Commission found that protesters’ arguments suggesting that the DLOL proposal did not provide sufficient information regarding the LSE Reserve Requirement calculation fell outside the scope of that proceeding because MISO “ha[d] sufficiently explained that LSE Reserve Requirements calculations will be maintained and account for the determination of UCAP based on the proposed DLOL accreditation methodology.”  We find that existing LSE Reserve Requirement calculations are not being revised and can similarly account for the changes proposed in this proceeding.  Accordingly, as in the DLOL Order, we find that LSE Reserve Requirements are beyond the scope of this proceeding.  Moreover, we note MISO’s intent to address the alignment of resource accreditation and LSE obligations in a separate proceeding, which MISO states will be implemented at the same time as the effective date requested for the instant proposal, following the conclusion of ongoing stakeholder discussions.
Additionally, we agree with MISO that no protester identifies a sufficient basis to justify postponing the instant proposal in favor of reforms to LSE Reserve Requirements calculations.  In particular, we are unpersuaded by ALLETE’s assertion that the instant proposal would render existing Tariff provisions unusable.  The Tariff can be changed in multiple iterations, as ALLETE acknowledges, and, because the instant proposal does not modify the determination of LSE Reserve Requirements, we do not find any conflicting Tariff provisions in this regard.  For this reason, we decline ALLETE’s request to reject the instant proposal in favor of MISO putting it forth concurrently with a future filing.  Similarly, we decline Steel Producers’ request to condition acceptance of the instant proposal on MISO’s future filing.
We find that MISO’s proposed use of, and method to determine, Capability is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  Specifically, we find that Capability is an accurate representation of the amount of energy that a resource can provide because Capability is capped at a resource’s Generation Verification Test Capacity or Capacity Rating, as applicable, and these values represent the amount of Demand reduction that the resource has attested, and MISO has verified, it can provide.  We also note that Capability is applicable to all demand-side resources, regardless of participation option.  By proposing four unique classifications for determining the Capability of resources participating as DRR-Type I or LMR, we find that MISO’s proposal is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential because it accommodates all resource types and baseline methodologies under these participation options in a standardized way using a common metric.  For similar reasons, we find that MISO’s proposed use of Seasonal Capability is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  In particular, we find that MISO, in distinguishing Business Days from non-Business Days and more heavily weighting Business Days to account for the more significant operations that occur on Business Days, creates a just and reasonable method to determine what a resource using the Firm Service Level baseline would have consumed had it not been deployed.
Accordingly, we are unpersuaded by protesters’ arguments challenging the use of Capability.  Although we acknowledge that there may be occasional instances in which a resource could offer Capability beyond its Capacity Rating, as Voltus asserts, we disagree that MISO is disincentivizing resource availability by instituting the Capacity Rating.  Instead, we believe that the Capacity Rating would reduce the over-accreditation of resources that may not be fully available when needed, which MISO explains is a challenge under its existing accreditation framework.  Moreover, we note that the Capacity Rating, by definition, is the amount of Demand reduction that a Demand Resource registers in the Auction, and that this amount is determined by the market participant each Season.  Thus, a market participant wishing to receive credit for a resource’s maximum availability need only register that amount in the Auction, but at the risk of reduced accreditation if the resource is unable to perform at that registered amount when called upon by MISO.  We also disagree with DTE Electric’s contention that the maximum Capacity Rating is ambiguous and could lead to the over-accreditation of a resource compared to other similarly situated LMRs.  Instead, we find that MISO’s proposal to collect certain meter data from DRRs and LMRs sufficiently clarifies the capabilities of a resource registered in the Auction, thus alleviating the concern raised by DTE Electric.
We are similarly unpersuaded by arguments from Steel Producers and Midwest TDUs that there is a requirement for Demand Resources under Schedule 53B to return to normal operations (i.e., their full Demand) within one hour after the end of a deployment.  As an initial matter, MISO states that it will not release resources until there is certainty that the resources are no longer needed to meet peak Demand, which we believe reduces the immediate likelihood of such resources being called on for a subsequent deployment.  We recognize, however, that resources that take more than one hour to resume normal operations after a deployment could face reduced accreditation after an Event concludes and grid conditions return to normal.  We further recognize that there may be instances when MISO deploys resources twice (or more) within a single day, and that resources that have difficulty resuming normal operations quickly could face reduced accreditation for not fully responding to a subsequent Event.  In such circumstances, we find that, because MISO has included the option for resources to Self Schedule during Capacity At Risk Hours, those resources concerned about reduced accreditation after an initial deployment may remain curtailed and receive accreditation either during Capacity At Risk Hours following a single Event or during Capacity At Risk Hours between Events.  While we acknowledge that the option to Self Schedule is not available during RA Hours that do not overlap with Capacity At Risk Hours, we find that this limitation is just and reasonable, as discussed below.
Additionally, we disagree with protesters’ assertions that the claimed one-hour requirement will lead to a widespread reduction in participation because, as discussed above, there are multiple participation options available for resources to choose from based on their operating characteristics.  Further, we find that MISO has demonstrated that one hour of additional accreditation post-deployment provides resources with the ability to improve their accreditation without materially reducing the incentive to voluntarily curtail Demand.  We therefore decline Steel Producers’ request to direct MISO to lengthen the time a resource receives higher Capability to six hours or, alternatively, to direct MISO to allow market participants to designate, prior to the beginning of the Planning Year, the time it typically takes a resource to ramp up.  We similarly decline Midwest TDUs’ request to allow a Demand Resource to demonstrate that a longer time is appropriate at the time of registration.
We find that MISO’s proposed use of Capacity Availability and Capacity Availability Thresholds is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  Specifically, we agree with MISO that Capacity Availability is appropriate because DRR-Type I and LMRs are not obligated to be available for all Emergencies, and that, by using Capacity Availability to indicate how much energy a resource has made available in real time, MISO is incentivizing resources to make themselves available during periods of greatest system risk.  Moreover, MISO proposes to cap Capacity Availability values at the registered Load Curve or submitted meter data, as applicable; therefore, we find that using Capacity Availability is just and reasonable because it is indicative of how much energy a Demand Resource has made available in real-time.  We also find that the proposed Capability adjustment, which modifies the Capability of a resource using the Firm Service Level baseline when the resource’s Capacity Availability is above or below certain Capacity Availability Thresholds, is just and reasonable because the Capability Adjustment will help determine the accuracy of responses that resources are required to provide.
We are unpersuaded by protesters’ arguments opposing the use of Capacity Availability or Capacity Availability Thresholds.  Specifically, we disagree with Advanced Energy and Midwest TDUs that the Capability adjustment disincentivizes participation and that the penalty for overstating expected future Demand is unjust and unreasonable.  As MISO explains, and we agree, the stricter penalties, along with reasonable Tolerance Bands, provide a balanced incentive to ensure that resources comply with the Tariff to address issues regarding the accuracy of submitted resource   availability information.  We therefore decline Advanced Energy’s request to direct MISO to eliminate the Tolerance Bands or, as Midwest TDUs request, to allow certain industrial loads to change their consumption plans at any time.  Additionally, we disagree with Midwest TDUs’ argument that the Capability adjustment results in undue discrimination or that the penalty for overstating expected future Demand is unjust and unreasonable.  All resources are subject to requirements regarding the accuracy of their submitted availability.  While resources using the Firm Service Level baseline are subject to different requirements than resources using other baselines regarding their submitted availability, we find that this differential treatment is not unduly discriminatory due to the unique operational characteristics and applicable performance requirements for resources that use the Firm Service Level baseline.  Specifically, the Firm Service Level baseline is the only baseline that measures a resource’s performance by confirming that a Demand Resource can reduce load to a certain amount.
We find that MISO’s proposed methodology for incorporating a Seasonal Emergency Hour Deficiency when accrediting Schedule 53B resources is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  For behind the meter generation resources, MISO’s proposal uses the existing methodology that MISO applies to Schedule 53A Resources; demand-side and supply-side resources thus have similar treatment.  Similarly, for Demand Resources, we find that MISO’s proposed methodology that uses either the Capacity Rating or Load Curve is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential because these values represent a resource’s registered performance ability, as submitted by a market participant during registration.  However, we agree with Midwest TDUs that MISO’s proposal to use the average of all Seasonal Capability values in a Season for a Demand Resource using the Firm Service Level baseline would equally weight Business Day and non-Business Day hours, resulting in distorted accreditation values that do not account for the fact that Business Days have a different reliability risk profile than non-Business Days, and, further, that there are significantly more Business Days per Season.  In its answer, MISO states that it will submit clarifications to backfill Seasonal Emergency Hour Deficiencies for Demand Resources that use the Firm Service Level baseline using only Business Days in the determination, if so ordered by the Commission.  Therefore, we direct MISO to file, within 30 days of the date of this order, a compliance filing to revise Schedule 53B to clarify the method to backfill Seasonal Emergency Hour Deficiencies for Demand Resources that use the Firm Service Level baseline using only Business Days in the determination, consistent with MISO’s offer in its answer.
We are unpersuaded by Steel Producers’ arguments that limiting accreditation for Self Scheduled load to reductions during Capacity At Risk Hours penalizes resources for legitimate local or non-emergency actions and would potentially disincentivize participation during critical times.  Instead, we find that such a limitation is not punitive because it aligns with the accreditation of resources based on their performance during periods of highest system risk for the MISO region, rather than routine or localized self-scheduling needs, and prevents over-accreditation.  We need not address Steel Producers’ alternative proposal to require MISO to accredit LMRs using Seasonal Capability when such resources Self Schedule in all Capacity At Risk Hours and RA Hours because we find that MISO’s proposed changes to Demand Resources’ ability to Self Schedule are just and reasonable. 
Lastly, we find that MISO’s proposal to exclude those behind the meter generation resources not registered as a Generation Resource or DRR-Type II from planned outage exemptions is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. Behind the meter generation (that is not registered as a Generation Resource or as DRR-Type II) is not similarly situated to other resource types because it is not obligated to participate in outage coordination with MISO, and, moreover, MISO cannot monitor or verify the status of such resources due to the lack of real-time telemetry and direct dispatch control, which MISO explains results in the inability for MISO to determine an adequate maintenance margin.  In other words, we find that it is reasonable for MISO not to accommodate planned outages within its capacity accreditation framework for resources that are not obligated to coordinate those outages with MISO.  Therefore, MISO reasonably balances its operational needs with a range of participation options that accommodate behind the meter generation resources.  Further, we note that MISO’s proposal does not prohibit all behind the meter generation resources from receiving a planned outage exemption.  Instead, MISO proposes distinct options for behind the meter generation resources to participate in MISO’s markets as demand-side resources, one of which allows for planned outage exemptions (i.e., DRR-Type II), while four other options do not (i.e., DRR-Type I, LMR-Type I, LMR-Type II, Non-Emergency BTMG).  Thus, a behind the meter generation resource that wishes to participate as a demand-side resource and receive a planned outage exemption may do so under the DRR-Type II participation option, provided that the resource meets the applicable requirements, including:  (1) economic and physical withholding provisions; (2) participation in planned outage coordination; and (3) real-time telemetry.
Although certain behind the meter generation resources may be ineligible for a planned outage exemption under MISO’s proposal, either because they cannot meet the DRR-Type II participation requirements or they prefer an alternative participation option, we do not believe that this ineligibility renders the instant proposal unjust and unreasonable or unduly discriminatory or preferential.  Each participation option has specific obligations and compensation mechanisms that do not depend solely on the type of resource, which, consistent with our finding above, creates non-discriminatory participation options for all behind the meter generation resources that wish to participate in MISO’s markets.  While we acknowledge that there are differences across the proposed participation options, particularly related to planned outage exemptions, we find that such differences reasonably balance the operational characteristics and unique capabilities of behind the meter generation resources with the need to ensure that accreditation reflects how often, and the level at which, these resources respond to MISO instructions.
Resource Classes
MISO’s Filing
MISO states that Resource Classes provide a forward-looking probabilistic estimate of a resource’s expected performance, but that it would be inappropriate to assign a Demand Resource to a Resource Class because such resources may perform the same tasks while having very different operating characteristics, thus rendering the benefits of the two-step DLOL methodology moot.  MISO proposes, therefore, to assign only behind the meter generation resources, regardless of participation option, and AME Resources to a Resource Class.  MISO explains that behind the meter generation resources will be accredited using the exact same Resource Class values that are used for Schedule 53A Resources to ensure that behind the meter generation resources’ expected contributions to resource adequacy are properly measured.  MISO states, however, that the determination of Resource Class values under Schedule 53A will not include behind the meter generation of any type to prevent such resources from either increasing or decreasing the accreditation of the applicable Resource Class.
Responsive Pleadings
Protests
Midwest TDUs argue that MISO does not adequately explain the inconsistent treatment of Resource Classes when accrediting behind the meter generation resources.  Specifically, Midwest TDUs assert that behind the meter generation resources are excluded from the calculation of Resource Class values, yet MISO proposes to use Resource Class values when accrediting behind the meter generation resources, such as when calculating Seasonal Emergency Hour Deficiencies.  Midwest TDUs assert that the Commission should require MISO to further explain why it is appropriate to use Resource Class-level data for the accreditation of behind the meter generation resources despite such resources being excluded from Resource Class-level data.  Midwest TDUs further argue that excluding behind the meter generation resources from Resource Class-level data may not reflect the availability of such resources, and, further, that it would be unfair to reduce the accreditation of behind the meter generation resources if the other resources used to develop Resource Class-level data are generally less available than behind the meter generation resources.  Midwest TDUs assert, therefore, that MISO should continue to accept individual unit data to backfill Seasonal Emergency Hour Deficiencies for behind the meter generation resources when such data are available.
Answers
MISO Answer
MISO disputes Midwest TDUs’ assertion that MISO does not adequately explain its inconsistent treatment of Resource Classes when accrediting behind the meter generation resources.  While MISO acknowledges that it is possible for an individual behind the meter generation resource to perform above or below Resource Class level performance, MISO argues that Midwest TDUs have not demonstrated why behind the meter generation resources, as a whole, should be considered to have performance above or below the average of Generation Resources.  Instead, MISO asserts that differences in accrediting behind the meter generation resources and Generation Resources creates a disconnect between the resources’ respective ISAC values.  MISO also notes that, when determining the Resource Class UCAP of behind the meter generation resources, such resources are either effectively modeled as Demand Resources (e.g., deployed only during Emergencies) or modeled as more traditional generation.  MISO contends that either of these reasons alone would preclude the inclusion of behind the meter generation resources into the Resource Class values to prevent there being a discrepancy between the number of MWs on each side of the equation.  MISO explains that, while it considered a case-by-case inclusion of behind the meter generation resources, doing so would cause equity concerns.
Additional Answers
Midwest TDUs argue that MISO’s answer fails to provide sufficient explanation for why it is reasonable to use Resource Class-level data based on the performance of non-behind the meter generation resources to accredit behind the meter generation resources.  Midwest TDUs assert that MISO makes a clear and relevant difference between Schedule 53A Resources and behind the meter generation resources in that the former are used to determine Resource Class-level data while the latter are not.  Midwest TDUs contend, therefore, that it is illogical to determine the accreditation of behind the meter generation resources based on Resource Classes that do not include any behind the meter generation resources, just as it would be illogical to determine the accreditation of a Schedule 53A Resource using Resource Class-level data from a different Resource Class.
Commission Determination
We find that MISO’s proposal to assign only behind the meter generation resources and AME Resources to a Resource Class is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  Notably, the Commission has previously found that assigning a resource to a Resource Class based on fuel type and similar operating characteristics is reasonable, and, moreover, that the DLOL methodology accredits all Resource Classes based on their expected ability to meet MISO’s resource adequacy needs and accounts for the differing performance of all resources within a Resource Class using the same metric.  Consistent with this prior finding, we agree with MISO that, because each Demand Resource has unique operating characteristics despite performing similar tasks, here it would be inappropriate to assign Demand Resources to a Resource Class as doing so could result in such a resource receiving accreditation that does not align with its Capability.
Similarly, we find that MISO’s proposal to accredit behind the meter generation resources using Schedule 53A Resource Classes, but not including such resources as part of the Resource Class calculations, is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential because such inclusion could result in accreditation values that do not align with the true performance capabilities of Schedule 53A Resources.  Despite Midwest TDUs’ assertion to the contrary, we agree with MISO that the diverse operational and situational characteristics of behind the meter generation resources, including being modeled as either a Demand Resource or a Generation Resource, makes it impractical to include such resources in Resource Class calculations.  We find, therefore, that MISO’s proposal standardizes the treatment of diverse behind the meter generation resources for accreditation purposes while also maximizing MISO’s ability to accredit all resources based on their specific operating characteristics and expected performance, and is therefore just and reasonable.
We are unpersuaded by Midwest TDUs’ argument that it is unreasonable to accredit behind the meter generation resources using Resource Class-level data from only Generation Resources.  We disagree with Midwest TDUs that behind the meter generation resources, as a whole, should be considered to have performance above or below the average of Generation Resources.  Moreover, we find nothing in the record to indicate that the Generation Resources used to develop Resource Class-level data are generally more or less available than behind the meter generation resources.  We need not address Midwest TDUs’ alternative proposal to require MISO to continue accepting individual unit data to backfill Seasonal Emergency Hour Deficiencies for behind the meter generation resources when such data are available because we find, as discussed above, that MISO’s proposal to accredit behind the meter generation resources using Schedule 53A Resource Classes is just and reasonable.
Availability Cap
MISO’s Filing
MISO explains that, unlike Schedule 53A Resources that are subject to physical and economic withholding provisions if they fail to submit an offer in the Day-Ahead Market, DRR-Type I and LMRs do not have the same obligations because their market participation is voluntary, and, as such, additional incentives are needed to ensure that these resources are accredited properly.  Consequently, MISO proposes an availability cap that is based on the proportion of Events for which DRR-Type I and LMRs are available compared to the total number of Events that occur.  Specifically, MISO explains that the availability cap accounts for the difference in resources’ availability while acknowledging that resources that are only available for some Events do not have the same Capacity value as resources that are available for all Events.  MISO states, therefore, that implementing an availability cap will provide an incentive for DRR-Type I and LMRs to be available that differentiates those individual resources with high availability from those with low availability.
As the IMM explains, MISO’s proposed availability cap acknowledges that DRR-Type I and LMRs still have capacity value even if they are not available for every Event, although a resource’s accreditation will be reduced by the portion of time that it is unavailable during a potential deployment.  MISO proposes, therefore, that, for resources participating as DRR-Type I or LMR, accreditation will be determined using the lesser of the availability cap or the values calculated using the resource’s Capability pursuant to the chosen baseline methodology.  MISO notes, however, that, because DRR-Type I and LMR are not obligated to be available for all Emergencies, these resources may receive accreditation calculated using the Capability of the resource during RA Hours that occur outside of Events.
According to MISO, determining the number of Events during a period of increased system risk is dependent on whether LMRs are deployed.  MISO explains that an Event is either an LMR deployment within the same LBA, or, if no LMR deployment occurs, a set of Capacity At Risk Hours during which an RA Hour occurs; however, if an LMR deployment occurs during a set of Capacity At Risk Hours, the LMR deployment overrides.  Further, MISO states that a resource is available for deployment during an Event for those hours when the resource has a Capability above zero, meaning the resource is Self Scheduled, makes itself available for deployment, or is operating at or below its Firm Service Level.  MISO explains that a resource needs to be available during all RA Hours that occur during an Event to receive credit for being available.  MISO states that it selected RA Hours to incentivize resources to be available when needed while also balancing stakeholder concerns about being available for every hour of a contiguous set of Capacity At Risk Hours, which may include overnight hours.
Responsive Pleadings
Comments in Support
COMPP argues that the availability cap would ensure that DRR-Type I and LMRs receive proper signals to remain under certain consumption levels.
Protests
Entergy Services, IMEA, and OMS claim that the availability cap may create uncertainty and have unintended consequences because resources would be required to respond to every Event, and for the full duration of each Event, regardless of length, or risk reduced accreditation.  They contend that, because availability for an Event requires participation in every hour of that Event, MISO would consider a resource unavailable even if it performed for nearly all of the Event, or, as IMEA points out, if a resource is able to perform but is prevented from doing so by exogenous circumstances.  IMEA claims, therefore, that MISO proposes to measure chance rather than performance such that, if resources are accredited less than they otherwise would be through the current accreditation methodology, MISO is signaling to market participants that resources will be penalized regardless of their ability to support the grid.

While OMS states that it expects MISO to revisit this element if, in practice, it appears overly burdensome without commensurate benefits, Entergy Services asserts that a more equitable result would be to consider a resource available for deployment based on a percentage threshold of the number of Emergency hours that the resource was available in a Season (e.g., 70%-80%).  Additionally, OMS argues that, because market participants would need to plan further in advance and forecast accurately to ensure that a resource is available to respond, it would be helpful to have additional information to make sound decisions about the risk of losing accreditation.  OMS requests, therefore, that MISO provides office hours or creates tools and calculators that would aid market participants in understanding their options and risks.

Entergy Services states that its understanding is that MISO should credit a resource as being available for an entire Event if the resource deploys for its minimum deployment duration (i.e., four hours), but that, under proposed Schedule 53B, a resource must have a “Capability greater than zero (0) during all Resource Adequacy Hours occurring within the Event” to be considered available.
Advanced Energy asserts that the availability cap limits accreditation based on the Load Curve or meter data.  Advanced Energy claims that MISO’s framework should incentivize high accreditation for resources with high availability, not, as MISO proposes, cap accreditation during an Event because doing so does not align accreditation with Capability during times of need.  Advanced Energy asserts that the Commission should direct MISO to remove the availability cap component of its proposal.
Voltus argues that, under the availability cap, it would be feasible for a new resource to enroll, set limited availability during critical windows, and earn payments despite not being available at times of highest system need at the simple cost of future-year accreditation.  Voltus further argues that the availability cap provides no opportunity for an LMR to improve its accreditation year-over-year if, for example, it experiences a legitimate outage during the only Event in a Season.  Instead, Voltus asserts that MISO’s market would be better served by introducing an availability requirement, wherein resources must demonstrate availability at or near accredited volumes during system Emergencies.  Voltus contends that resources unable to meet this availability requirement should be required to either replace “shortfall” Zonal Resource Credits or, for any unreplaced capacity, “buy out” of their capacity shortfall at the Seasonal Zonal Auction Clearing Price.  Voltus asserts that availability penalties and capacity “buy out” options are typical in other wholesale electricity markets, including NYISO, which requires in its demand response capacity constructs buy-outs at the auction clearing price for undelivered MWs, and ERCOT, which reduces payments to market participants in the event of failed availability assessments at the aggregate level.
Answers
MISO Answer
In response to Entergy Services’ and Voltus’ concerns with the proposed availability cap, MISO states that it considered requiring availability across a select number of hours but concluded that opportunities existed for market participants to satisfy this requirement while minimizing their probability of being deployed.  For example, MISO explains that a resource with a six-hour notification time may be unavailable to deploy when LMRs requiring a six-hour lead time are deployed, but this same resource could achieve a non-zero Capability for a portion of the accredited hours by making itself available for deployment after an hour or two have passed, even though, as a practical matter, the resource was unavailable.  MISO explains that it addressed these concerns by restricting availability to only RA Hours during a declared Emergency rather than requiring availability across all accredited hours.  MISO contends that this approach establishes a strong incentive for resources to be available, thus ensuring that they are deployable, while acknowledging that imperfect availability across all accredited hours will not result in an adverse reduction to accreditation.
MISO further argues that concerns regarding availability after a deployment are unfounded.  MISO reiterates that, by definition, a set of continuous Capacity at Risk Hours during which a deployment of LMRs occurs will only have the availability cap during hours in which LMRs deploy.  MISO states that, once a resource has met its obligation to respond for at least four hours, the resource has satisfied its requirement for the purposes of the availability cap.  MISO asserts that its operators will not release LMRs until there is certainty that the resources are no longer required to meet peak demand, and, in the event of two deployments in a single day, LMRs would be expected to deploy for both events or face reduced accreditation.  MISO argues that this is just and reasonable because a resource capable of deploying for all Events should receive more accreditation than a resource that cannot deploy for all Events.  MISO notes, however, that resources with difficulty consuming load between deployments are incentivized to remain curtailed and would receive accreditation as a Self-Scheduled Resource, meaning a Capability greater than zero, and so would be considered fully available.
MISO argues that Voltus’ assertions that MISO’s proposal should be rejected or modified in favor of approaches used in other RTOs/ISOs are not relevant to the instant proceeding because:  (1) under section 205, MISO need only show that its proposal is just and reasonable, not that its proposal is better or more just and reasonable than the approaches of other RTOs/ISOs; and (2) the Commission has allowed RTOs/ISOs to develop tailored rules and market design elements to account for regional differences, and, as such, the Commission’s approval of one approach in PJM does not preclude the Commission from approving a different approach in MISO.  Additionally, in response to assertions from OMS about the “complexity” of the instant proposal, MISO argues that this complexity is not inherently problematic because MISO’s proposal accommodates the competing needs of both MISO and its stakeholders.
Commission Determination
We find that the proposed availability cap is a just and reasonable mechanism to accredit resources with Emergency-only obligations because basing the availability cap on historical availability and performance during periods of highest system risk ensures that resources are compensated based on their actual reliability contribution to resource adequacy.  By design, the availability cap is determined using a Demand Resource’s Capacity Rating, which is the amount of Demand reduction that a market participant registers in the Auction each Season, or, alternatively, the ICAP for BTMG, and the number of Events to which a resource responds in a Season.  We agree with MISO that the availability cap provides a strong incentive for resources to be available, and, moreover, that those resources that are available for an Event, but choose not to respond, should receive a lower accreditation than resources that respond to all Events.
We are unpersuaded by arguments that the availability cap may create uncertainty or have unintended consequences by incentivizing resources to fully respond to every Event.  While we agree with protesters that variations in the number and duration of Events across Seasons will correspondingly affect resources’ accreditation, we believe that such differences reflect the inherent unpredictability of Emergencies, not any purported uncertainty resulting from the availability cap, as it is difficult to accurately forecast the timing, duration, or severity of an Event.  Moreover, in claiming that MISO would penalize resources that do not fully perform during an Event, regardless of the cause of any underperformance, we believe that protesters overlook a key objective of MISO’s proposal that we agree will support resource adequacy:  ensuring that accreditation reflects how often resources respond to Emergencies and the level at which they respond.  Thus, rather than subjecting resources to chance or limiting accreditation based on the Load Curve or meter data, as IMEA and Advanced Energy suggest, respectively, we find that the availability cap creates a standard framework to assess the performance of individual resources during Events, regardless of temporal duration or other differentiating factors, such that individual resources receive accreditation for the performance they actually provide.  Furthermore, we note that, while there may be other just and reasonable methods to calculate capacity accreditation values using different levels of risk tolerance, the fact that MISO proposes the availability cap to measure a resource’s performance in response to an Event, rather than other potentially reasonable approaches, does not make the proposal unjust and unreasonable.
We need not address alternative proposals raised by Advanced Energy, Voltus, or Entergy Services because we find, as discussed above, that MISO’s proposed availability cap is just and reasonable.  In addition, we are unpersuaded by Entergy Services’ assertion that MISO’s proposal does not consider how to determine resource availability for the hours immediately following a MISO Scheduling Instruction.  As MISO explains, and consistent with our reasoning above, in the event of two deployments in a single day, a resource would be expected to deploy for both Events or face reduced accreditation.
However, we agree with Entergy Services that it is unclear how MISO will determine if a resource has “fully met” a Scheduling Instruction or Setpoint Instruction in certain circumstances.  Specifically, the methodology for determining hourly Capability values, and, subsequently, the potential application of the availability cap, remains unclear under proposed Schedule 53B for a resource that successfully deploys for the first four hours of a six-hour Event but fails to fully deploy for the last two hours of that Event.  MISO explains in its answer that, “[o]nce a resource has met its obligation to respond for at least four hours, the resource has met its requirements for the purposes of the availability cap;” however, we note that section III.A.4 of proposed Schedule 53B provides that “a resource is considered available for deployment during an Event if it has a Capability greater than zero (0) during all Resource Adequacy Hours occurring within the Event.”  Accordingly, we direct MISO to file, within 30 days of the date of this order, a compliance filing to revise its Tariff to clarify how it will determine if a Demand Resource has “fully met a Setpoint Instruction or Scheduling Instruction” under section III.A.1.c of Schedule 53B for purposes of calculating that resource’s Capability, consistent with MISO’s answer.
Lookback Period
MISO’s Filing
MISO explains that, under the second step of the DLOL methodology, MISO uses historical resource-level performance to accredit individual Schedule 53A Resources, and that all of these resources are subject to a three-year lookback period.  MISO argues that it is appropriate to use a similar three-year lookback period for AME Resources and DRR-Type II because these resources have the same availability obligations as Schedule 53A Resources and must submit offers in the Day-Ahead Market during all hours.  MISO similarly argues that a three-year lookback period is appropriate for Non-Emergency BTMG because these resources provide Capacity value at all hours of the year and only receive accreditation when they inject energy.  Accordingly, MISO proposes that AME Resources, DRR-Type II, and Non-Emergency BTMG use the three most recent periods between September 1 and August 31 for their respective lookback periods.
MISO proposes a one-year lookback period for DRR-Type I and LMRs, and argues that doing so is just and reasonable because it ensures that a strong signal to be available is sent without creating the possibility of a Season with reduced availability overly impacting resources’ accreditation.  MISO explains that the flexibility in availability provided to DRR-Type I and LMRs, which does not exist for Schedule 53A Resources, DRR-Type II, or AME Resources, requires sending strong signals while still giving DRR-Type I and LMRs the ability to make changes to improve their accredited values each year.  MISO argues that, if a three-year lookback period was used, a DRR-Type I or LMR may encounter years in which it does not have the ability to improve its accreditation, regardless of its availability.  MISO contends, therefore, that using a one-year lookback period for DRR-Type I and LMRs ensures that they maintain flexibility in deployment, which MISO asserts that stakeholders indicated was a desirable property of these resources, while not being subject to potentially overly punitive accreditation penalties due to the availability cap.  Accordingly, MISO proposes that DRR-Type I and LMRs use the most recent period between September 1 and August 31 for their respective lookback periods.
MISO explains that the choice of the appropriate lookback period depends on the underlying nature of the resource type subject to MISO’s proposal.  However, the IMM states a preference for a three-year lookback period rather than the one-year lookback period proposed by MISO.  The IMM contends that the incentive effects of the two lookback periods are comparable because, while non-performance under a one-year lookback period will produce a larger accreditation impact the next year, non-performance under a three-year lookback period will affect a market participant by a smaller amount for a longer timeframe.
The IMM also states that the greater accreditation volatility of the one-year lookback period is unnecessary and may create inefficient market outcomes.  In particular, the IMM contends that there will be a smaller sample of hours under the one-year lookback period because some Seasons are likely to have no Capacity At Risk Hours.  According to the IMM, this means that resources’ Capability would be calculated in other hours that are a less accurate reflection of the Emergency conditions when resources are needed, which would increase the likelihood that a resource’s accreditation is substantially understated in some years and substantially overstated in other years.  The IMM continues to support MISO’s proposal, however, because it believes that MISO’s proposal as a whole is far superior to MISO’s current Tariff provisions.

Protests
Multiple protesters argue that MISO should use a three-year lookback period for DRR-Type I and LMRs because the proposed one-year lookback period is more volatile and could reduce resources’ accreditation.  Protesters assert that the IMM explains the benefits of the three-year lookback period when compared to the one-year lookback period, including a larger historical data set that accounts for performance across multiple years, which commenters contend will lead to more accurate and stable accreditation of DRR-Type I and LMRs.  In particular, Midwest TDUs dispute MISO’s assertion that the one-year lookback period “ensures that a strong signal to be available is sent” because, as the IMM states, “the incentive effects of the two lookback periods are equivalent.”  Midwest TDUs assert, therefore, that the only difference is the time over which the same capacity and financial impacts are concentrated, and that, by condensing those impacts by using the one-year lookback period, MISO merely creates unnecessary volatility without changing the overall incentives.  Additionally, while AMP agrees with the IMM’s rationale for a three-year lookback period, AMP argues that the IMM, in concluding that MISO’s proposal is superior to MISO’s current Tariff provisions, provides no justification for the unnecessary, discriminatory treatment of LMRs.
AMP, Entergy Services, and Midwest TDUs also argue that using a three-year lookback period for DRR-Type I and LMRs aligns with MISO’s treatment of Schedule 53A Resources.  AMP and Midwest TDUs claim, however, that MISO fails to demonstrate that the imposition of the one-year lookback period for DRR-Type I and LMRs is not unduly discriminatory, including, as Midwest TDUs point out, for behind the meter generation resources that are similar to Schedule 53A Resources.  AMP asserts that MISO’s proposed accreditation of LMRs using the one-year lookback period should be rejected because it is inconsistent with the treatment that MISO proposes for Schedule 53A Resources, DRR-Type II, and Non-Emergency BTMG.

BTMG Utilities argue that MISO, in proposing the one-year lookback period, fails to recognize that dispatchable behind the meter generation resources provide capacity and energy to the grid during all hours of the year and during Emergencies.  Similarly, Midwest TDUs reject MISO’s assertion that behind the meter generation resources have “flexibility in availability” that requires an incentive through the one-year lookback period because any unavailability of these resources is already factored into their accreditation through the availability cap.

Midwest TDUs further assert that volatility in accreditation would cause volatility in capacity payments to behind the meter generation owners, which may discourage the participation of both existing and new behind the meter generation resources in MISO’s capacity construct.
Answers
MISO Answer
MISO asserts that the Commission should not be persuaded by multiple commenters’ selective references to the IMM’s preference for a three-year lookback period.  MISO claims that the IMM’s affidavit makes it clear that the IMM supports the instant proposal, notwithstanding the IMM’s position on the lookback period.
MISO argues that the choice of a three-year lookback period versus a one-year lookback period comes down to an evaluation of the signal sent to a resource to be available, which, according to MISO, is balanced by the requirement that resources may be provided the opportunity to take positive actions to improve their accreditation.  MISO asserts, however, that a three-year lookback period for resources with an obligation to only be available during Emergencies does not properly align resource incentives with ensuring reliability.  MISO explains that, unlike resources that serve load during all periods, a resource that is only available during Emergencies requires an availability incentive because the risk of involuntary load shed increases if that resource is not available during an Emergency.  Moreover, MISO contends that ratepayers could hardly be faulted for questioning the need to compensate a resource to reduce load if that resource later fails to reduce load.
MISO asserts that the combination of infrequent Events, when added with the flexibility of the availability cap, requires MISO to strongly signal to resources to make themselves available as much as possible.  Thus, MISO states that, while it agrees that a three-year lookback period is likely to provide more stability, the tradeoff is an inability to improve accreditation on the more immediate basis that the one-year lookback period provides.  Ultimately, MISO states that it agrees with those commenters claiming that resources should be able to take steps to improve their accredited values each year.
MISO argues that there are three reasons why the benefits of a one-year lookback period outweigh the potential risk of increased volatility.  First, MISO asserts that resources could experience a sum total loss of accreditation under the three-year lookback period, despite taking actions to make themselves more available in some years, that would be greater than what would be experienced under the one-year lookback period.  Second, MISO states that the potential penalties for being unavailable are greater under a three-year lookback period because irregular conditions could negatively affect accreditation by a larger amount over time when compared to a one-year lookback period.  Third, MISO asserts that a three-year lookback period does not signal all resources to be available as strongly as a one-year lookback period because, as the availability cap is a cap on accreditation and not a reduction of accreditation, no signal is sent if a resource’s expected accreditation is below this cap.  Accordingly, MISO argues that the signal to be available is non-existent for a resource with a certain maximum accredited value under a three-year lookback period, while the one-year lookback period continues to send a signal to be available.

Commission Determination
We find that MISO’s proposed one-year lookback period for DRR-Type I and LMRs is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  We find that a one-year lookback period incentivizes DRR-Type I and LMRs to be available during periods of highest system risk.  Specifically, we agree with MISO that a one-year lookback period provides a strong signal for DRR-Type I and LMRs to make themselves available during Emergencies while also providing flexibility in deployment, thus strengthening resources’ responsiveness and availability across the MISO system by aligning accreditation with resources’ most recent performance.  Moreover, we find that it is just and reasonable to ensure that DRR-Type I and LMRs are available during periods of highest system risk through the application of the one-year lookback period because such resources are among the last to be dispatched before load shed occurs. 
We are unpersuaded by arguments that the one-year lookback period is less beneficial than the three-year lookback period.  As an initial matter, MISO need not demonstrate that its proposal is the most just and reasonable approach, or that its approach is better than an alternative.  Thus, despite protesters’ assertions that the benefits of the three-year lookback period outweigh those of the one-year lookback period, the question before us is whether MISO has demonstrated that the one-year lookback period is just and reasonable, and, for the reasons described above, we find that it is.  Similarly, we are unpersuaded by Midwest TDUs’ argument that the benefits identified by MISO of the one-year lookback period relative to the three-year lookback period are without merit because, even if these benefits were not substantiated (although we believe that they are), the absence of such benefits alone would not demonstrate that the one-year lookback period is unjust and unreasonable.
Regardless, we disagree with arguments that the one-year lookback period, when compared to the three-year lookback period, creates unnecessary volatility without changing overall incentives, including for behind the meter generation resources.  While we recognize that the one-year lookback period may introduce some variations in year-to-year accreditation when compared to a three-year lookback period, we do not believe that such variations are inherently unstable or otherwise result in unnecessary volatility.  Instead, we agree with MISO that, given the importance of ensuring the availability of DRR-Type I and LMRs during Emergencies, any fluctuations in year-to-year accreditation are an acceptable tradeoff because they are reflective of a resource’s ability to respond to, and improve, its accreditation on a more immediate basis under the one-year lookback period.
We are also unpersuaded by arguments that applying the one-year lookback period only to DRR-Type I and LMRs is unduly discriminatory.  Although certain protesters assert that the one-year lookback period is inconsistent with MISO’s proposed treatment of DRR-Type II and Non-Emergency BTMG, we find that MISO justifies the use of different lookback periods by differentiating both the eligibility and participation requirements for DRR-Type II and Non-Emergency BTMG, which are non-Emergency resources, from those of DRR-Type I and LMRs, which are Emergency resources.  Specifically, we find that this differential treatment is just and reasonable because, unlike other participation options, DRR-Type I and LMRs are only obligated to be available during Emergencies, and therefore providing an incentive tied more closely to recent performance will help ensure that such resources are available specifically during Emergencies.  Moreover, and as previously discussed, we agree with MISO that the specific obligations and compensation mechanisms of each participation option are not dependent on the type of resource.
For similar reasons, we find unavailing arguments that the one-year lookback period is unduly discriminatory because Schedule 53A Resources are subject to the three-year lookback period.  Specifically, we disagree with certain protesters that behind the meter generation resources are similarly situated to Schedule 53A Resources.  As MISO explains, and we agree, Schedule 53A Resources that clear the Auction are obligated to offer into the Day-Ahead Market whereas DRR-Type I and LMR are only obligated to respond during Emergencies and may make themselves unavailable at the cost of reduced accreditation.  Thus, we find that MISO justifies the use of different lookback periods by clearly differentiating the performance requirements of Schedule 53A Resources from those of DRR-Type I and LMRs.
Resource Accreditation Methodologies
MISO’s Filing
DRR-Type I and LMR Accreditation
MISO explains that DRR-Type I and LMR-Type I may elect to make themselves unavailable for any reason without facing sanctions, but that being unavailable may reduce accreditation, including if they are unavailable for the only Event in a Season.  MISO states that, in contrast, LMR-Type II must always be available to provide Demand reduction in response to Scheduling Instructions during an Emergency.  Accordingly, MISO proposes that the pre-grossed-up SAC value for a Demand Resource participating as DRR-Type I or LMR equals the lesser of:  (1) the ISAC value, which is calculated for each Season based on a resource’s Capability during each Capacity At Risk Hour and Seasonal RA Hour; or (2) the availability cap, which multiplies a resource’s Capacity Rating by the sum of the number of Events for which a resource is available by the total number of Events within the same LBA.  Similarly, MISO proposes that the pre-grossed-up SAC value for BTMG resources participating as DRR-Type I or LMR equals the lesser of:  (1) the ISAC value, which is calculated each Season based on Resource Class-level UCAP and Resource Class-level ISAC; or (2) the availability cap, which multiplies an individual BTMG resource’s ICAP by the sum of the number of Events for which the resource is available by the total number of Events within the same LBA.
MISO proposes that, to calculate final SAC values, the preliminary accreditation values for both Demand Resources and BTMG resources are grossed-up by the amount of avoided transmission losses, with Demand Resources’ preliminary accreditation values also being grossed-up by the applicable Planning Reserve Margin (PRM).  MISO explains that it currently calculates a gross-up for transmission line losses and the PRM pursuant to section 68A.8.b and section 68A.2 of the Tariff, respectively.
MISO states that DRR-Type I and LMRs use Capacity At Risk Hours and RA Hours as these resources are only required to deploy during Emergencies, and, as a result, accrediting them across all hours of the year would misalign their accreditation and performance.  Additionally, MISO explains that, when there are fewer than a combined 65 Capacity At Risk Hours and RA Hours in a Season, each missing hour will be calculated based on the chosen Measurement and Verification methodology of the DRR-Type I or LMR, except for BTMG resources, which use the same methodology as Schedule 53A Resources.  MISO states that a one-year lookback period will be used to accredit DRR-Type I and LMRs.
Non-Emergency BTMG Accreditation
MISO states that Non-Emergency BTMG resources operate continuously behind the meter to offset load and do not have any specific performance obligations.  MISO explains that these resources must inject energy to receive accreditation, which provides a strong performance incentive as they will not receive accreditation when they are not producing.  MISO states that, because Non-Emergency BTMG resources do not submit Offers or otherwise make themselves available to respond to MISO instructions, they are not subject to an availability cap.  Instead, MISO explains that Capability will be determined using the metered output to calculate ISAC, and, further, that MISO will cap the hourly Capability values at the Generation Verification Test Capacity, as is done for Schedule 53A Resources.  Thus, MISO proposes that the pre-grossed-up SAC value of Non-Emergency BTMG resources will be calculated as the product of Resource Class-level UCAP and the division of the resource’s ISAC by Resource Class-level ISAC, and that this value will be grossed-up by the amount of avoided transmission line losses to calculate the final SAC value.
MISO states that Non-Emergency BTMG resources will use all hours of the year to determine accreditation, with RA Hours weighted in the same manner as Schedule 53A Resources.  MISO explains that Non-Emergency BTMG resources will be assigned to a Resource Class such that, if there are fewer than 65 RA Hours in a Season, Non-Emergency BTMG resources will fill in the missing values using the Resource Class UCAP as a percentage of the corresponding Resource Class ICAP multiplied by the BTMG ICAP.  MISO states that a three-year lookback period will be used to accredit Non-Emergency BTMG.
DRR-Type II Accreditation
MISO explains that, as DRR-Type II is obligated to offer into the Day-Ahead Market and is subject to economic and physical withholding provisions, it is not subject to an availability cap.  Instead, MISO states that Capability will be determined by using the submitted Offer in each hour, as is done for Schedule 53A Resources, and that Capability will be capped in a given hour at the registered Capacity Rating or Generation Verification Test Capacity, as applicable.
MISO proposes that the final SAC value for DRR-Type II backed by a Demand Resource will be the ISAC value, which is calculated using Tier 1 ISAC and Tier 2 ISAC values, grossed-up by the amount of avoided transmission line losses and by the applicable PRM.  Similarly, MISO proposes that the final SAC value for DRR-Type II backed by a behind the meter generation resource will be calculated as the product of Resource Class-level UCAP and the division of the resource’s ISAC by Resource Class-level ISAC, which is then grossed-up by the amount of avoided transmission line losses.
MISO states that DRR-Type II will use all hours of the year to determine accreditation, with RA Hours weighted in the same manner as Schedule 53A Resources.  MISO explains that DRR-Type II backed by behind the meter generation will be assigned to a Resource Class such that, if there are fewer than 65 RA Hours in a Season, accreditation will be determined in the same manner as Schedule 53A Resources (i.e., using the Resource Class UCAP as a percentage of the corresponding Resource Class ICAP multiplied by the BMTG ICAP for the missing hours below the 65-hour threshold).  MISO states that, for DRR-Type II backed by a Demand Resource using the calculated baseline, each missing RA Hour below the 65-hour threshold will be determined using the Capacity Rating.  Additionally, MISO states that a three-year lookback period will be used to accredit DRR-Type II.
AME Resource Accreditation
MISO states that a resource, other than a DRR-Type I, will be accredited as an AME Resource under Schedule 53B when it qualifies as an AME Resource in at least 110 Hours in a Season in either the Day-Ahead Market or the Real-Time Market.  MISO explains, however, that a resource with AME Resource status in 109 or fewer hours in the Day-Ahead Market and 109 Hours or fewer in the Real-Time Market will be accredited as a Schedule 53A Resource.
MISO states that an AME Resource under Schedule 53B will be assigned to a Resource Class so long as it is not a DRR-Type II that is backed by a Demand Resource.  MISO explains that, as AME Resources that clear the Auction are obligated to offer into the Day-Ahead Market and are subject to economic and physical withholding provisions, they are not subject to an availability cap.  Instead, MISO explains that Capability for an AME Resource accredited under Schedule 53B will be determined using the submitted Offer in each hour, as is done for Schedule 53A Resources, and that Capability will be capped in a given hour at the registered Capacity Rating or Generation Verification Test Capacity, as applicable.  Thus, MISO proposes that the SAC value of AME Resources accredited under Schedule 53B will be calculated as the product of Resource Class-level UCAP and the division of the resource’s ISAC by Resource Class-level ISAC.
MISO states that an AME Resource accredited under Schedule 53B will use Capacity At Risk Hours and RA Hours to reflect the Emergency status these resources have elected.  MISO explains that, when there are fewer than 65 RA Hours in a Season, an AME Resource will fill in the missing values in the same manner as Schedule 53A Resources (i.e., using the Resource Class UCAP as a percentage of the corresponding Resource Class ICAP multiplied by the Resource ICAP).  Additionally, MISO states that AME Resources are subject to a three-year lookback period, which MISO explains is to prevent destabilizing resources’ accreditation when going from a Schedule 53A Resource in one period to a Schedule 53B Resource in another period, and because these resources are not subject to the availability cap.

Commission Determination
We find that MISO’s proposed resource accreditation methodologies for DRR, LMR, BTMG, Non-Emergency BTMG, and AME Resources are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential because, as discussed above, we find that there are substantial similarities between proposed Schedule 53B and the Commission-approved DLOL methodology provided for in Schedule 53A.  Specifically, Schedule 53B aligns the accreditation of demand-side resources with the DLOL methodology such that resources are accredited based on their availability and actual contributions to reliability and resource adequacy.  Where there are differences, MISO sufficiently explains that such changes are needed to account for the operating characteristics and performance obligations that differentiate demand-side resources from supply-side resources.
We disagree with protesters that the proposed accreditation of behind the meter generation resources is unjust and unreasonable or otherwise unduly discriminatory or preferential.  As an initial matter, we find that protesters’ preference for an alternative accreditation option does not render the options included in MISO’s proposal unjust and unreasonable.  Moreover, we agree with MISO that, under the proposed accreditation methodology, behind the meter generation resources continue to have the option to participate in the Auction as either a DRR-Type II or Generation Resource.  MISO’s proposal includes two additional accreditation options for behind the meter generation resources that choose to participate in the capacity market (i.e., BTMG resources, Non-Emergency BTMG resources).
We further disagree with Advanced Energy’s argument that MISO’s proposed accreditation requirements would categorize partial failures as complete failures, and that doing so is punitive.  MISO’s proposal only references partial and complete failures in the context of a MISO-initiated test of a resource, not the performance of a resource in response to MISO instructions, as Advanced Energy claims.  Further, we note that MISO’s proposed reforms to LMR non-performance penalties, which MISO has filed in Docket No. ER26-1882-000, include performance evaluation criteria to categorize LMR underperformance as either a partial failure or complete failure.  Thus, we agree with MISO that Advanced Energy’s concerns related to partial and complete failures are outside the scope of this proceeding.
Testing
MISO’s Filing
MISO states that, under its current framework, resources are not required to be tested other than the self-performed tests necessary to participate in the Auction.  MISO explains that approximately one-third of the total registered Demand reduction ability of Demand Resources never experience a test of any kind because market participants may opt out of these tests in exchange for facing higher penalties.  MISO asserts, therefore, that MISO-initiated testing is necessary because:  (1) the Enforcement Orders identified behavior that could have been recognized and alleviated earlier with testing provisions; and (2) MISO and the IMM identified instances of non-existent resources registering in the Auction.  Thus, MISO argues that MISO-initiated testing would dissuade and identify these types of behaviors due to certainty of receiving Scheduling Instructions.
Consequently, MISO proposes to test all Demand Resources and resources that reduce Demand participating in the Auction.  MISO states that DRR-Type I, DRR-Type II, and LMR-Type I will be tested once every three years while LMR-Type II will be tested annually.  MISO explains that a resource that has successfully responded to a MISO instruction will have that response count as the MISO-initiated test, but that there are no opt out provisions for resources other than LMR-Type II.  MISO clarifies that only LMR-Type II that have successfully responded to all deployment instructions and MISO-initiated tests in the previous three years will be permitted to qualify for this opt out, and, further, that these resources are subject to certain penalties if they fail to respond to MISO instructions.
MISO also states that it proposes annual testing for resources that are large aggregations.  MISO explains that annual testing of large aggregations is needed because end-use customer contracts are more difficult to track due to the volume of contracts, which can lead to gaming in the registration process and ultimately poses a risk to reliability.  MISO asserts that an annual testing requirement strongly disincentives registering large aggregations without underlying contracts in the Auction, thus ensuring that aggregated resources are registered in an appropriate manner.
MISO explains that it will notify market participants at least 24 hours prior to conducting a test, and that market participants will have the opportunity to reschedule one test, which must be performed within the earlier of 30 days or within the same Season.  MISO states that it may initiate a test during any part of a four-hour window that will be designated at the time of the test notification, taking into consideration the resource’s notification time.  MISO explains that a resource is not required to provide its full registered amount of Demand reduction, and that a test is successfully passed if a market participant is able to meet the Scheduling Instruction within the notification time and hold the Demand reduction for the full four-hour period.

Therefore, MISO asserts that providing the additional notice recommended by Steel Producers would not be as close to a Scheduling Instruction as possible.

Deficiency Letter and Responses
Deficiency Letter
The Deficiency Letter asked MISO to identify the specific Tariff language in proposed Tariff section 69A.3.8.1.a that distinguishes those Demand Resources using a Statistical Measurement and Verification methodology, and are therefore subject to a MISO-initiated test once per Planning Year, from those Demand Resources that do not use a Statistical Measurement and Verification methodology, and are therefore subject to a MISO-initiated test once every three Planning Years.
MISO Answer
In its Deficiency Response, MISO points to the phrase “using a[n] [Attachment TT] Statistical Measurement and Verification Methodology” in proposed Tariff section 69A.3.8.1.a.i to distinguish the testing frequency provisions.  MISO states that, at the time of registration for the Auction, a market participant selects which baseline its resource will use.  MISO explains that a DRR or LMR-Type I using a Statistical Measurement and Verification methodology baseline is subject to an annual testing requirement and that proposed Tariff section 69A.3.8.1.a.i applies.  MISO further explains that a DRR or LMR-Type I that selects any other baseline that is not explicitly defined as a Statistical Measurement and Verification baseline, as set forth in section 3 of Attachment TT, is subject to the once every three years testing requirement in proposed Tariff section 69A.3.8.1.a.ii.  MISO asserts that, as there is specific language indicating the distinction between those Demand Resources subject to proposed Tariff sections 69A.3.8.1.a.i and 69A.3.8.1.a.ii, the two testing provisions do not conflict.
Protests
Midwest TDUs argue that the proposed Tariff language is still unclear because MISO did not modify proposed Tariff section 69A.3.8.1.a.ii to reflect MISO’s clarification that DRR-Type I, DRR-Type II, and LMR-Type I selecting a Statistical and Measurement Verification methodology would be tested annually while those resources that select any other baseline would be tested once every three years.  Instead, Midwest TDUs assert that the language in proposed Tariff section 69A.3.8.1.a.ii covers all DRR-Type I, DRR-Type II, and LMR-Type I, regardless of the baseline selected.  Midwest TDUs argue that, although they do not object to MISO’s intended outcome, market participants should be able to understand the essential requirements of participating in MISO’s markets (e.g., the required testing frequency) from the plain language of the Tariff rather than needing to “sift through MISO’s pleadings” to resolve ambiguity or divine MISO’s intent.
Commission Determination
We find that MISO’s proposed testing provisions are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential, subject to certain clarifications, as discussed below.  As a general matter, we agree with MISO that MISO-initiated testing will help identify potential market manipulation and detect non-existent resources registered during the early stages of the Auction.  We also agree that such testing will enhance certainty for MISO regarding resource performance and response capability.
We find that MISO’s proposed 24-hours’ notice for testing is just and reasonable because, as MISO explains, this notification period ensures that testing simulates a resource’s real-time response to MISO instructions during an Emergency and confirms the resource’s ability to respond, consistent with its registered notification time.  Accordingly, we are unpersuaded by arguments opposing MISO’s proposed 24-hours’ notice for testing.  Moreover, because MISO submitted its proposal pursuant to section 205, the Commission must only consider whether the use of 24-hours’ notice is just and reasonable, not whether an alternative is more or less reasonable.  Thus, despite protesters’ assertions that other RTOs/ISOs employ different notification procedures, we may only consider the justness and reasonableness of MISO’s proposal to use 24-hours’ notice for testing.  Having found that MISO’s proposed 24-hours’ notification is just and reasonable, we therefore decline to consider such arguments as well as Steel Producers’ request for the Commission to require an alternative, three-phase notification process.
We find that MISO’s proposal to require market participants to sustain a four-hour deployment is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential because it represents the minimum threshold for Demand Resources to participate in the Auction.  We further find that it is just and reasonable for MISO to require market participants that seek to be compensated for responding to MISO instructions to demonstrate the ability to satisfy a four-hour minimum deployment, as doing so provides a reasonable mechanism to verify a resource’s ability to perform when called.  Accordingly, we are unpersuaded by protesters’ arguments that the proposed four-hour test is unduly burdensome.  Similarly, we decline to consider alternative proposals suggested by protesters, including different testing durations employed by other RTOs/ISOs.
We find that MISO’s proposal to test DRR-Type I, DRR-Type II, and LMR-Type I that are not using a Statistical Measurement and Verification methodology once every three years, while testing LMR-Type II and resources using a Statistical Measurement and Verification methodology annually, is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential, subject to certain clarifications.  Specifically, we find that MISO’s proposal aligns testing frequency with a participation option’s applicable performance requirements and considers a resource’s chosen Measurement and Verification methodology.
However, we agree with Midwest TDUs’ concern regarding the ambiguity in proposed Tariff section 69A.3.8.1.a.ii as to whether the requirement to test certain resources once every three years applies to all DRR-Type I, DRR-Type II, and LMR-Type I, regardless of the baseline selected, or only to those resources that do not elect a Statistical Measurement and Verification methodology, given that proposed Tariff section 69A.3.8.1.a.i imposes an annual testing requirement on resources using a Statistical Measurement and Verification methodology.  For example, it is not clear whether an LMR Type-I that elects a Statistical Measurement and Verification methodology will be subject to annual testing or testing once every three years.  We recognize MISO’s explanation that the proposed annual testing requirement for Demand Resources that use a Statistical Measurement and Verification methodology in proposed Tariff section 69A.3.8.1.a.i is meant to be controlling, independent of the specific resource type; however, notwithstanding MISO’s explanation, we find that the proposed Tariff language does not clearly identify which provision takes precedence.  Therefore, we also find that proposed Tariff sections 69A.3.8.1.a.i and 69A.3.8.1.a.ii are in direct conflict with one another.  Accordingly, we direct MISO to file, within 30 days of the date of this order, a compliance filing clarifying Tariff section 69A.3.8.1.a.ii  to provide that resources participating as DRRs or LMR-Type I and not using the Statistical Measurement and Verification methodology will be tested once every three years, consistent with MISO’s intent, as stated in its answer and Deficiency Response.
We agree with Midwest TDUs that the proposed Tariff language does not reflect MISO’s stated intent to reschedule one test within the earlier of 30 days or within the same Season.  Accordingly, we direct MISO to file, within 30 days of the date of this order, a compliance filing to clarify this provision, consistent with MISO’s offer in its answer.
We further agree with Midwest TDUs that the proposed Tariff language does not clearly state that a full registered amount of Demand reduction is not required during testing.  We therefore direct MISO to file, within 30 days of the date of this order, a compliance filing to clarify this requirement, consistent with MISO’s offer in its answer.
The Commission orders:

MISO’s proposed Tariff revisions are hereby accepted, subject to condition, effective September 1, 2027, as requested, as discussed in the body of this order.

MISO is hereby directed to submit a compliance filing within                    30 days of the date of this order, as discussed in the body of this order.

Commissioner Chang is dissenting with a separate statement  attached.
